\(P(a=1\mid b=0)\) and \(P(b=1\mid a=1)\). The second is Bayes with two causes.
Same posterior if \(p(b)=10^{-3}\). What did raising the prior do?
The radio reports a small earthquake. Does \(P(b=1\mid a=1,r=1)\) go up or down from \(P(b=1\mid a=1)\)? Why, in two sentences, and why is that not “the alarm was a false positive”?







TipSolution






\(P(a=1\mid b=0)=0.1\cdot 0.01=0.001\). Then \[
P(b=1\mid a=1)=\frac{2\cdot 10^{-4}}{2\cdot 10^{-4}+0.001\cdot(1-2\cdot 10^{-4})}\approx 0.167.
\]
About \(0.50\). A larger prior on burglary, with the same likelihood, raises the posterior. That is Bayes, not a new alarm model.
Down. The radio is an alternative cause of the same alarm (explaining away). The sensor still sounded; burglary is just no longer the remaining explanation.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
text:
Problem 12. Holes you can see
Lab 2 Exercise 3; Wald.
316 planes returned. Cockpit: 36 returned, 21 down. Engine: 29 returned, 31 down. Someone counted 36 cockpit holes on the planes that came back and wants cockpit armor.

Among the planes you can see, how common is cockpit damage?
Among planes that took a cockpit hit, how often did the plane come back? Same question for engine.
Which of those numbers goes in the brief? One sentence on what \(36/316\) is actually describing.







TipSolution






\(36/316\approx 0.114\).
Cockpit: \(36/57\approx 0.63\) came back. Engine: \(29/60\approx 0.48\).
Armor goes where returning was rare given the hit. The 11% is holes on the planes you can see. The 63% vs 48% is the decision.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
text:
Problem 13. Name the count
Lab 3 Exercise 2.
For each, say Binomial or Poisson, and why.

80 independently tested circuit boards. \(X=\) number that fail.
Cardiac-arrest calls to 911 between midnight and 6am.
A subscriber is shown 12 thumbnails. \(X=\) number they click. Each click independent with the same \(p\).
Goals Hull scores against Man U on Saturday.







TipSolution






Binomial: a list of 80 independent yes/no trials.
Poisson: a rate, no list of trials.
Binomial: 12 independent clicks.
Poisson: a rate of goals, not 90 independent minute-trials with a fixed \(p\).

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
text:
Problem 14. Four at-bats
Lab 3 Exercise 3, first number. Lecture self-check.
Joe DiMaggio, \(p=0.325\) per at-bat. Treat four at-bats as independent Bernoulli trials.

Name the distribution of \(X=\) hits in a game.
Write \(P(X>2)\) as two binomial terms, then compute it. Do not paste \(0.104\) from a slide.
What did independence do for you, and what would a hit raising the next \(p\) do to this probability?







TipSolution






\(X\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(4,0.325)\).
\(P(X=3)+P(X=4)=\binom{4}{3}(0.325)^3(0.675)+(0.325)^4\approx 0.0927+0.0112=0.104\).
Independence lets the pmf factor. A hit raising the next \(p\) raises \(P(X>2)\): the mass on 3 and 4 hits moves up relative to the independent calculation. The 56-game streak is this 10% stacked, not a typical night.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
text:
Problem 16. Warranty
Lab 4 Exercise 1.
Life \(L\sim N(10,3^2)\) years. The warranty pays if \(L<5\). A shipment has 80 independent components.

\(p=P(L<5)\). Write the \(z\)-score. Name the distribution of \(X=\) number of claims in the shipment, and write \(E(X)\).
If lives have a heavier left tail than this Normal, which way does \(E(X)\) move? Which of the two models did you change, and which did you keep?







TipSolution






\(z=(5-10)/3=-5/3\approx -1.67\), so \(p=\Phi(-1.67)\approx 0.048\). \(X\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(80,p)\), \(E(X)=80p\approx 3.8\).
A heavier left tail raises \(p\), so \(E(X)\) rises. You changed the model for \(L\). The binomial layer that turns \(p\) into a count is the same.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
section: Problem 17. A month in the book
text:
Problem 17. A month in the book
Lab 4 Exercise 2.
Monthly return \(X\sim N(0.008,0.035^2)\).

\(P(X<-0.08)\).
\(z\)-score of a \(-12\%\) month.
The \(1\%\) quantile of \(X\).
The officer wants \(P(X<-0.08)=0.05\) without changing the mean. What \(\sigma\) would that take? Use \(\Phi^{-1}(0.05)\approx -1.645\), not \(1.96\).
The 1987 crash was a 5-sigma month under a Normal fitted to earlier data. Is \(P(X<-0.08)\) under the Normal too small, too large, or could it go either way?







TipSolution






\(z=(-0.08-0.008)/0.035=-2.51\), so \(P\approx 0.006\).
\(z=(-0.12-0.008)/0.035\approx -3.66\).
\(q=0.008+0.035\cdot\Phi^{-1}(0.01)\approx -0.073\).
\((-0.08-0.008)/\sigma=-1.645\) gives \(\sigma\approx 0.0535\). The book’s \(0.035\) is too tight if a probability of \(0.05\) for an \(8\%\) decline is the risk the officer wants to price.
A heavier-tailed histogram than the bell makes far-left probabilities larger than the Normal says, so \(0.006\) is too small. That is the crash lesson, not a maybe.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
section: Problem 17B. The histogram is not a bell
text:
Problem 17B. The histogram is not a bell
Lecture: Normal tails; Lab 4 Exercise 2. Same monthly returns as Problem 17, now as a picture.
The histogram is 80 months. The dashed curve is \(N(0.008, 0.035^2)\), the model from Problem 17, scaled to the same bins.





Monthly returns. Histogram of 80 months; dashed curve is the Normal used in Problem 17, scaled to the same bins.





Where does the histogram disagree with the dashed curve? (The dotted vertical line is \(-8\%\), the event in Problem 17a.)
Is \(P(X<-0.08)\approx 0.006\) from the Normal too small, too large, or could it go either way?
Collecting 800 months instead of 80, still from this world, would make the histogram look more like the dashed curve. True or false, and what did you just assume?







TipSolution






The centre is a bit too peaked, and both tails have mass the Normal put at nearly zero. Several months sit left of \(-8\%\), where the dashed curve is already on the floor.
Too small. The left tail of the histogram is heavier than \(\Phi(-2.51)\).
False. A larger \(n\) makes the histogram closer to the true density, which here is not Normal. The dashed curve is the wrong model, not a noisy estimate of the right one. The 1987 lesson is the same: more months will not manufacture a bell. The eight months left of \(-8\%\) are already a larger left tail than \(\Phi(-2.51)\approx 0.006\) allows.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
text:
Problem 18. A large count
Lab 4 Exercise 3.
\(n=400\) people, each buys independently with \(p=0.12\). \(X=\) number who buy.

Name the distribution of \(X\). Write \(E(X)\) and \(\mathrm{sd}(X)\).
Using the Normal with that mean and sd, \(P(X\ge 60)\) is \(P(Z\ge ?)\). What is the \(z\)? You may leave the tail as \(1-\Phi(z)\).
Why is a Normal even in the conversation? The \(X_i\) are 0–1.







TipSolution






\(X\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(400,0.12)\). \(E(X)=48\), \(\mathrm{sd}(X)=\sqrt{400\cdot 0.12\cdot 0.88}=\sqrt{42.24}\approx 6.50\).
\(z=(60-48)/6.50\approx 1.85\). \(P\approx 1-\Phi(1.85)\).
CLT: a sum of many independent Bernoulli trials is approximately Normal. The binomial is already that sum. You are not claiming each person is Normal.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
section: Problem 19. CDF and a leftover delivery
text:
Problem 19. CDF and a leftover delivery
Book Chapter 1, Conditional Probability (delivery times).
Delivery day \(X\in\{1,\ldots,7\}\) with CDF



\(x\)
1
2
3
4
5
6
7




\(P(X\le x)\)
0.10
0.20
0.70
0.75
0.80
0.90
1




Fill \(P(X=x)\).
\(P(X=4\mid X\ge 4)\).







TipSolution






Differences of the CDF: \(0.10,0.10,0.50,0.05,0.05,0.10,0.10\).
\(P(X=4\mid X\ge 4)=0.05/(1-0.70)=0.05/0.30=1/6\).

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
text:
Problem 19B. Read \(F\)
Lab 5 Exercise 1. Lecture: eight calls, then the die.
Eight calls took \(0.4, 0.6, 0.9, 1.1, 1.5, 1.8, 2.4, 3.1\) seconds. The timeout is 2 seconds. \(F(x)=P(X\le x)\).

Empirical \(F(2)\) from these eight calls.
A model says the next call is \(\mathrm{Uniform}(0,4)\), so \(F(x)=x/4\) on \([0,4]\). What is \(F(2)\) under the model? The sample said \(0.75\) and the model says \(0.50\). Which number is for the next call, and what did you assume about these eight?
A fair die. \(F(2)\), \(F(4)\), and \(F(4)-F(2)\). Does that difference include a 2? What is \(P(2\le X\le 4)\)?







TipSolution






Six of the eight times are at most 2, so \(F(2)=6/8=0.75\).
\(F(2)=2/4=0.5\). The \(0.75\) describes these eight calls. The \(0.50\) is the next call only if the next one is a draw from \(\mathrm{Uniform}(0,4)\). A continuous model also has \(P(X=2)=0\), even though \(F(2)\) is not zero.
\(F(2)=2/6\), \(F(4)=4/6\), \(F(4)-F(2)=2/6\). That is \(2<X\le 4\): the jump at 2 sits in \(F(2)\), so it is not in the difference. \(P(2\le X\le 4)=3/6\).

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
text:
Problem 21. Bernoulli likelihood
Book Chapter 11, MLE for Bernoulli.
\(y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\{0,1\}\), \(P(Y=1)=\theta\).

Likelihood \(L(\theta)\).
Log-likelihood \(\ell(\theta)\).
Write \(-\ell(\theta)\) for a single observation \(y\). Where have you met it before?







TipSolution






\(L(\theta)=\theta^{\sum y_i}(1-\theta)^{n-\sum y_i}\).
\(\ell(\theta)=\sum y_i\log\theta+(n-\sum y_i)\log(1-\theta)\).
\(-y\log\theta-(1-y)\log(1-\theta)\): the log loss of predicting \(\theta\) for an observation \(y\). Summed over the data it is \(-\ell(\theta)\), so minimizing the total log loss is the same as maximizing the likelihood. That is how logistic regression is fitted.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
section: Problem 23B. The average, not the call
text:
Problem 23B. The average, not the call
Lab 5 Exercise 4. Lecture: standard error falls with \(\sqrt{n}\).
Hold times are Exponential with mean 2 minutes, so one hold has \(\sigma=2\) and a long right tail. The dashboard pages when the average of the last \(n\) holds exceeds 2.5 minutes. Nothing is wrong with the line.

\(\mathrm{sd}(\bar X)\) at \(n=5\), \(n=20\), and \(n=80\). What does going from 20 to 80 do to that standard error?
Treat the average of 80 holds as \(N(2,\sigma^2/80)\). Write \(P(\bar X>2.5)\) as \(1-\Phi(z)\) and give \(z\).
One hold time is not Normal. Why is the Normal in (b) still the right picture at \(n=80\), and where would you refuse it?







TipSolution






\(2/\sqrt{5}\approx 0.89\), \(2/\sqrt{20}\approx 0.45\), \(2/\sqrt{80}\approx 0.22\). From 20 to 80 is four times the data, so the standard error is cut in half.
\(z=(2.5-2)/(2/\sqrt{80})=\sqrt{80}/4\approx 2.24\). \(P\approx 1-\Phi(2.24)\).
The CLT is about the average, not about one Exponential draw. At \(n=80\) the histogram of averages is close to that Normal; at \(n=5\) the skew is still there and the Normal page rate is the wrong picture.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
section: Problem 24. OLS and a residual plot
text:
Problem 24. OLS and a residual plot
Book Chapter 12, Residual Analysis and OLS Derivation (d).
lm(price ~ sqft)     # price in $1000s

(Intercept)  50.23    (se 12.35)
sqft          0.1234  (se 0.0089)
Residual se  45.67 on 98 df
R-squared     0.662

Interpret the slope in dollars per square foot.
Predicted price for a 2,000 sq ft house.
For simple regression, \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\). What does that say \(\hat\beta_1\) is made of?
A residual plot against fitted values shows a clear parabola. What would you do, and why is \(R^2=0.66\) not an argument to keep the linear model?







TipSolution






Each additional square foot is associated with \(\$123.40\) in predicted price.
\(50.23+0.1234\cdot 2000=297.03\) thousand, about \(\$297{,}000\).
It is the sample covariance of \(x\) and \(y\) over the sample variance of \(x\). The slope is a scaled association, not a causal claim.
A parabola in the residuals means the linear mean is wrong. Add a square, or log \(y\), or log-log, and look at the new residuals. \(R^2=0.66\) can be large while the mean is still bent; \(R^2\) does not see the pattern in \(e\) vs \(\hat y\).

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
section: Problem 24B. Who is in the sample
text:
Problem 24B. Who is in the sample
The same price ~ sqft fit is on 100 houses that sold last year.

Name two modelling assumptions besides “the mean is linear in sqft.”
Houses that did not sell are missing. If unsold houses are larger and overpriced, which way is \(\hat\beta_1\) pulled relative to the slope for listed houses?
You will use \(\hat y\) to advise a seller on asking price. What would have to be true for that use, and what would make you refuse?







TipSolution






The 100 sales are like draws from the population you care about (iid). Errors have constant variance. sqft is not standing in for omitted size-correlates (lot, school, renovation) that you will not have at prediction time.
Large unsold houses sit above the sold cloud in asking price but never enter \(y\). The sold line is fitted only on houses whose price was accepted. That usually flattens or tilts the sold slope relative to listed asking prices: you see completed trades, not the full asking curve. The direction to write: \(\hat\beta_1\) is a slope among accepted prices, so it is not the slope of list price on sqft.
The advice is for a house that will sell on the same market as last year’s sales. Refuse if the house is in a different segment (new build, distressed, a size outside the 100) or if the residual plot already said the linear mean is wrong. The \(R^2\) does not settle this.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
text:
Problem 24C. MSE or MAE
Book Chapter 11, MSE vs MAE.
Predictions \(\hat y=(2,3,4,5,20)\), actual \(y=(2,4,4,6,6)\).

MSE and MAE.
Which metric did the \(20\) dominate, and what assumption about the cost of error is MSE making?
For house prices, when would you report MAE rather than OLS?







TipSolution






Errors \(y-\hat y\): \(0,1,0,1,-14\). \(\mathrm{MSE}=(0+1+0+1+196)/5=39.6\). \(\mathrm{MAE}=(0+1+0+1+14)/5=3.2\).
MSE. Squaring treats a $14 miss as 196 times a $1 miss. That is the right loss if big misses are disproportionately costly (and if you believe the Normal likelihood, which is the same square).
When a few mansions or data errors should not own the fit: listing prices, a median asking price, or when the residual plot already shows a heavy tail. OLS/MSE is the default only if that square is the loss you actually have.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
text:
Problem 24D. Four residual plots
Book Chapter 12, Residual Analysis (d); lecture PGA and mammal residual checks.
Each panel is residuals against fitted values from lm(y ~ x) on \(n=80\) points. The same axes labels on all four.





Residuals versus fitted values. Four different data-generating stories, one linear fit each.





For each panel, name the pattern in one phrase (none / curved mean / non-constant variance / one outlier).
Which modelling assumption of OLS failed in B, in C, and in D? (A is the control.)
You need a price at \(x=8\). In which panel do you refuse the linear \(\hat y\), and in which do you keep the line but change the loss or how you talk about uncertainty?







TipSolution






A none (random scatter around 0). B curved mean (a U or parabola). C non-constant variance (spread grows with fitted). D one large positive residual.
B: \(E(y\mid x)\) is not linear in \(x\). C: constant variance. D: least squares / MSE treats that point as an ordinary miss; it is not. A is the case where those three are still plausible.
Refuse B: the line is the wrong mean, so \(\hat y\) at \(x=8\) is systematically off. Keep the line in C and D only with a change of use: in C report a spread that grows with \(x\), or transform; in D use MAE, or drop a data error after you have named it, rather than let one point own \(\hat\beta\). \(R^2\) is not in any of the four pictures, and would not have told B from A.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
section: Problem 25. Log-log as a power law
text:
Problem 25. Log-log as a power law
Book Chapter 12, Log Transformations. Same move as mammal brain/body and Apple growth in lecture.
Advertising \(x\) and revenue \(y\) (both in $millions) follow \(y=ax^b\). Data: \((x,y)=(1,5),(2,8),(4,14),(8,25),(16,45)\).
A log-log fit gives \(\log y=1.564+0.798\log x\) (natural logs).

Transform the power law to a linear model.
What are \(\hat a\) and \(\hat b\)? Interpret \(b\).
Predict revenue at \(x=10\).
Why might you prefer this to OLS of \(y\) on \(x\) in the original scale, even if the raw \(R^2\) looks fine?







TipSolution






\(\log y=\log a+b\log x\).
\(\hat b=0.798\), \(\hat a=e^{1.564}\approx 4.78\). A 1% increase in advertising is associated with about a 0.80% increase in revenue: diminishing returns. Doubling \(x\) multiplies \(y\) by \(2^{0.798}\approx 1.74\), not \(2\).
\(\hat y=4.78\cdot 10^{0.798}\approx 30.0\) million.
The original scale is multiplicative and the residual spread usually grows with \(x\). Log-log makes the mean linear and often gives constant variance. \(R^2\) on the raw scale is not comparable to \(R^2\) on the log scale, and a high raw \(R^2\) can hide the non-constant variance.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
text:
Problem 25B. Two scatters, same \(n\)
Book Chapter 12, Log Transformations; lecture mammal brain/body and Apple.
Advertising \(x\) and revenue \(y\), 60 campaigns. Left: \(y\) against \(x\) with the OLS line. Right: \(\log y\) against \(\log x\) with its OLS line.





Left: revenue against advertising, linear fit. Right: the same campaigns after a log-log transform.





What does the left plot say about \(E(y\mid x)\) and about \(\mathrm{Var}(y\mid x)\)?
Why is the right plot the same power-law model after a log-log transform, not a different theory of revenue?
The left-hand \(R^2\) is large. Is that an argument to keep the linear model?







TipSolution






The mean is bent (diminishing returns) and the vertical spread grows with \(x\) (non-constant variance). Both are the signature of a multiplicative \(y=ax^b\varepsilon\). The spread is the easier one to see; the curve is why the left-hand line overshoots the middle campaigns.
\(\log y=\log a+b\log x+\log\varepsilon\) is \(y=ax^b\) written so that OLS can see a straight mean. The slope on the right is \(b\). You did not switch from “revenue depends on advertising” to a new mechanism; you took logs until the mean was linear.
No. A large \(R^2\) can sit on a bent mean with non-constant variance. The residual plot (or the left scatter itself) is the check. Same lesson as Problem 24d and as the mammal plot in lecture.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
text:
Problem 26. Dummy variables
Lecture: \(k\) levels, \(k-1\) columns.
A house has style \(\in\{\text{colonial}, \text{ranch}, \text{split}\}\). You fit \[
\mathrm{price}=\beta_0+\beta_1\mathrm{sqft}+\beta_2\mathbf{1}_{\mathrm{ranch}}+\beta_3\mathbf{1}_{\mathrm{split}}+\varepsilon.
\]

Why not three style dummies plus an intercept?
What is \(\beta_2\)? What house is \(\beta_0+\beta_1\mathrm{sqft}\) describing?
You recode and drop ranch instead of colonial. Which fitted values change? Which coefficients change?







TipSolution






You cannot put three style columns and an intercept into a sum: every house is colonial or ranch or split, so the three 0/1 columns add to 1. That is why you need \(k-1\) columns. The omitted style is the reference.
\(\beta_2\) is the difference in expected price between ranch and colonial, at the same sqft. The intercept line is colonial.
Fitted values do not change. If you change the reference, every coefficient changes and the fitted values do not. You cannot compare \(\beta_2\) across the two fits without translating.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
text:
Problem 26B. Two clouds, one line
Lecture dummy variables; same house-price setting as Problem 26.
Left: ranch and colonial on the same scatter, one OLS line through all 80 houses. Right: the same points, two parallel lines (one intercept per style, common slope on sqft).





Price against living area. Grey: colonial. Black: ranch. Left: one line. Right: two intercepts, common slope.





What is the single line on the left averaging, and why is that slope the wrong rate for a ranch?
What did the dummy do on the right that the left plot could not?
You will quote \(\hat\beta_{\mathrm{sqft}}\) to a seller. Which plot’s slope do you send, and what would make you refuse even the right-hand picture?







TipSolution






It is a compromise between two clouds that sit in different parts of the sqft range. Ranch is larger and more expensive, so the pooled line climbs from colonial on the left to ranch on the right. The dollars-per-square-foot on the left is partly a style mix, not a size effect.
It let the intercept jump for ranch and kept a common slope. The vertical gap is \(\beta_{\mathrm{ranch}}\), the number Problem 26 asked for.
Send the right-hand slope, with the style named. Refuse if the two clouds are not parallel (style changes the rate, not just the intercept), if “ranch” is standing in for lot or school, or if this house is not in the same market as these 80 sales. Same sample warning as 24B.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
section: Problem 27. True or false, linear regression
text:
Problem 27. True or false, linear regression
Book Chapter 12, True/False: Linear Regression. Also Book Chapter 11, MSE vs MAE (c)–(d).

OLS minimises the sum of absolute residuals.
If \(y_i=x_i^T\beta+\varepsilon_i\) with iid Normal errors, MLE for \(\beta\) is OLS.
MAE is more affected by a single huge residual than MSE is.







TipSolution






False. OLS is squared residuals. Absolute residuals are MAE.
True. The Normal log-likelihood is \(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum(y_i-x_i^T\beta)^2\) plus a constant.
False. MSE squares the residual; the outlier dominates MSE more than MAE.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
section: Problem 28. From log-odds to a probability
text:
Problem 28. From log-odds to a probability
Book Chapter 13, Sigmoid. You need the function, not a derivative.
\(\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})\). A fitted log-odds is \(z=-0.5+0.4x\).

What is \(p\) at \(x=0\)? At \(x=0\), what does \(z=0\) mean when it occurs?
Show, in one line, that \(\sigma(-z)=1-\sigma(z)\). Why does that matter for a “no event” probability?
If \(x\) increases by 1, what happens to the odds? To \(p\)? (The second answer is not a constant.)







TipSolution






\(z=-0.5\), \(p=\sigma(-0.5)\approx 0.378\). \(z=0\) means \(p=1/2\), a coin flip under the model, which here is at \(x=0.5/0.4=1.25\), not at \(x=0\).
\(1-\sigma(z)=e^{-z}/(1+e^{-z})=\sigma(-z)\). \(P(\text{no event})=1-p=\sigma(-z)\).
Odds are multiplied by \(e^{0.4}\approx 1.49\). Probability follows the sigmoid, so the same \(+0.4\) in log-odds moves \(p\) a lot near \(0.5\) and almost not at all near \(0\) or \(1\).

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
text:
Problem 29. Log-odds
Book Chapter 13, Log-Odds Interpretation.
\[
\log\frac{p}{1-p}=-1.5+0.8\,\mathrm{usage}-2.0\,\mathrm{annual}.
\] annual \(=1\) for an annual contract, \(0\) for month-to-month. Usage in hours.

\(P(\text{churn})\) for 5 hours, month-to-month.
Odds ratio for switching to annual, usage held fixed.
How much would usage need to rise to double the odds of churning?
A product manager hears “annual cuts churn by 2.0.” What did they mix up, and what sentence would you send instead?







TipSolution






Log-odds \(= -1.5+4=2.5\), \(p=\sigma(2.5)\approx 0.924\).
\(e^{-2}\approx 0.135\). Annual multiplies the odds of churn by \(0.135\), an 86% reduction in odds, not a 2-point drop in probability.
\(e^{0.8\Delta}=2\) gives \(\Delta=\log 2/0.8\approx 0.87\) hours.
\(-2.0\) is a log-odds coefficient. The probability drop depends on where you start on the sigmoid. Send: “holding usage fixed, an annual contract multiplies churn odds by \(0.14\).” Then give \(p\) at a usage the manager actually has.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
text:
Problem 30B. What the coefficient assumed
A logistic default model on last year’s book: \[
\log\frac{p}{1-p}=-3.0+0.02\,\mathrm{balance}-0.8\,\mathrm{student}.
\] student \(=1\) if the borrower is a student.

Holding balance fixed, what did the model assume the \(-0.8\) is?
Students have higher balances on average. If you drop balance and refit with student alone, which way does the student coefficient typically move, and what assumption just failed?







TipSolution






It assumed that, at the same balance, students have lower log-odds of default than non-students. That is not “being a student causes lower default.”
The student coefficient typically rises (becomes less negative, or positive). Students look riskier in the margin because they carry more balance. The assumption that failed is that the student comparison is at the same balance.

title: AII 600 midterm problem bank
text:
Problem 31. True or false, logistic
Book Chapter 13, True/False: Logistic Regression.

A logistic coefficient is the change in probability for a one-unit increase in the predictor.
The odds ratio \(e^{\beta}\) can be negative.







TipSolution






False. It is a change in log-odds. Probability is the sigmoid of that.
False. \(e^{\beta}>0\) always. It can be less than 1.

title: On Hilbert’s 6th Problem Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation
text:
Description
In 1900 David Hilbert asked for a mathematical treatment of the axioms of physics, beginning with probability and mechanics, and for the limiting processes that lead from the atomistic view to the laws of motion of continua. This book follows that program, with Henri Poincaré as a central figure: Kolmogorov’s axioms, de Finetti’s theorem and Sanov’s large deviation theorem; ergodic theory and the method of types; Brownian motion, entropy and Nelson’s stochastic mechanics; kinetic theory, Lanford’s theorem and the passage from the Boltzmann equation to the Navier Stokes equations.
It then adds the inverse passage, from observed fluids back to the states that produced them. Part IV treats the inverse problem of a partial differential equation as Bayesian estimation on its solution manifold. For linear equations the adjoint evolution of the data is a sufficient statistic; for nonlinear equations it is asymptotically sufficient under a uniform Bernstein von Mises statement that the book states and leaves open. The cost of generative computation depends on the dimension that the data can resolve, and examples and experiments cover the heat, Navier Stokes and Schrödinger equations.
The last part treats inference itself as statistical mechanics: spin systems and Lee Yang zeros, Schrödinger bridges and generative Bayesian computation, gates as approximate nonlinear filters, and the thermodynamics of information. A final chapter lists open problems and builds a bridge to Hilbert’s eighth problem through the de Bruijn Newman heat flow. Every chapter closes with exercises, and the Python code behind the computed figures and tables is in the repository.

title: On Hilbert’s 6th Problem Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation
Books
text:
Books by Vadim Sokolov and coauthors. Each book is free to read as a PDF, and its source and code are on GitHub.


 Nicholas G. Polson and Vadim Sokolov. 2026. Edition 1.
Computes the Thorin measure whose positivity is equivalent to the Riemann Hypothesis, from Pólya’s integral for Xi in certified ball arithmetic, and proves that finite positivity tests on the heat trace cannot decide it; with hitting times, friable approximants, the reciprocal zeta function and Lee Yang theory.
   



 Nick Polson and Vadim Sokolov. 2026. Edition 1.
N queens counting as a rare event and a quantile integral, turned into a Monte Carlo program for P versus NP: NP = RP is shown equivalent to sampling queens completions, promise RP = promise P, which implies P = RP, is restated as a hitting set problem, with exact computations on the queens.
  



 Nick Polson and Vadim Sokolov. 2026. Edition 1.
A textbook that develops Bayesian reasoning, statistical learning and deep learning as one probabilistic framework, from Bayes’ rule and decision theory to neural networks, transformers and AI agents, with code in R and Python.
   



 Alexandra Sokolova and Vadim Sokolov. 2026. Edition 1.
Clinical trials as science and as regulated operations: design and statistics, the daily work of a Phase III study from site selection to the trial master file, regulatory submission, and what AI agents may and may not do in regulated research.
    



 Nicholas G. Polson. 2026. Edition 1.
Statistical theory of population genetics: an exact form of Fisher’s Fundamental Theorem, shrinkage estimates of the rate of adaptation, the Ewens sampling formula and its rigidity, rational conjugacy, and sufficiency for learned coalescent inference.
  



 Nick Polson and Vadim Sokolov. 2026. Edition 1.
What probability can and cannot contribute to the Langlands programme: Sato Tate laws, random walks on trees and isogeny graphs, Thorin measures and generalized gamma convolutions as reformulations of the Riemann hypothesis, and Bayesian identification of Sato Tate groups, with code and data.
   



 Nick Polson and Vadim Sokolov. 2026. Edition 1.
Why the Collatz (3x+1) conjecture resists proof: the map as a random walk, an optimizer and a Diophantine problem; proofs that fixed horizon monotone Lyapunov certificates and finite residue sieves cannot settle it and the cycle inequality cannot exclude all cycles; a momentum method from log2 3.
   



 Nick Polson and Vadim Sokolov. 2026. Edition 1.
Hilbert’s sixth problem from Kolmogorov’s axioms and the Boltzmann equation to the Navier Stokes equations, and the inverse passage: Bayesian estimation on the solution manifold of a differential equation, where the adjoint evolution of the data is a sufficient statistic for linear equations.

title: On Hilbert’s 6th Problem Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation
text:
Main results

Adjoint representation of the sufficient statistic (Lemma 15.1, page 206): For a linear evolution equation that is diagonal in a fixed basis, the data statistic that is sufficient for the initial state is the coefficient vector of the time zero value of the solution of the backward adjoint equation driven by the data as point sources.
Exact sufficiency, linear case (Proposition 15.2, page 207): In the linear model with a Gaussian prior the adjoint statistic is sufficient, the posterior given it is the full data posterior, and the conditional quantile map is exactly affine with slope equal to the posterior covariance.
Equivalence of the one step efficient score summary with the efficient centering (Proposition 15.5, page 210): Under explicit regularity, rate and Lipschitz conditions, the cross fitted one step efficient score summary agrees with the efficient centering of Nickl’s Bernstein von Mises theorem to order smaller than the root N scale in a negative Sobolev norm, so it is a computable center of the Gaussian limit of the posterior.
Jiang Wong under a uniform Bernstein von Mises assumption: the posterior mean summary is asymptotically sufficient (Theorem 15.38, page 256): If a Bernstein von Mises theorem holds uniformly over prior typical truths, then conditioning on the posterior mean alone, or on any summary root N equivalent to it, loses nothing at the root N scale: the recentered posterior given the summary and the recentered posterior given all of the data have the same Gaussian limit in Wasserstein distance. Status: conditional on the uniform Bernstein von Mises assumption (Assumption U).
Effective dimension under dissipation (Theorem 15.46, page 267): For the heat and Stokes equations on the torus with a power law prior, the number of modes in which the data at least halve the prior variance grows like a power of the sample size divided by viscosity times observation time, so dissipation lowers the effective dimension; for a nonlinear forward map, under a uniform Bernstein von Mises hypothesis and assumptions on the training residuals and the summary, a generator need only learn the posterior scale on those modes (in the linear model it needs no training), and the cost of using the prior spread beyond them is bounded explicitly. Status: conditional on Assumption U and other hypotheses of the quantile generator theorem, in part (ii) for nonlinear maps.
Transfer of Bernstein von Mises guarantees to the GBC posterior (BvM for GBC) (Theorem 16.2, page 275): If the posterior produced by a generative Bayesian computation (GBC) generator is closer to the exact posterior than the root N scale in Wasserstein distance and concentrates on the localization set with bounded moments, then it inherits the Bernstein von Mises limit of the exact posterior for the initial condition and, for the reaction diffusion and two dimensional Navier Stokes equations, for the trajectory, with exact asymptotic coverage of its credible bands and, for Navier Stokes, attainment of the local asymptotic minimax bound for bounded losses; nothing is assumed about how the generator was trained.
No uniform guarantee: minimax lower bound for conditional quantile generators over monotone Hölder classes (Theorem 16.15, page 290): Any generator, trained on M simulated pairs, that must be accurate at a fixed interior summary value for every conditional law in a monotone Hölder class of conditional quantile maps of smoothness beta on a J dimensional summary has, for some map in the class, Wasserstein error at least a constant free of J times (C M) to the power minus beta over (2 beta plus J) with probability at least 1/8, where C bounds the design density, so root N accuracy uniformly over the class requires at least N to the power 1 plus J over (2 beta) simulations divided by C, more than any polynomial once J grows; reading this as the accuracy condition of the transfer theorem uses the uniform Bernstein von Mises assumption.

title: Results by chapter On Hilbert’s 6th Problem

The results of On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation that are new in the book, that come from the authors’ own papers, or that correct one of those papers, as the book states them: 92 entries (59 proved, 11 conditional, 21 open, 1 counterexample). Results of other authors that the book presents are credited in the chapter summaries.
Status: proved; conditional (proved assuming the named statements, which the book does not prove); open (stated as an open question); counterexample (a proved counterexample); withdrawn (found wrong after release; the entry says what was wrong and which version corrects it).





Theorem 7.5, page 85 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. First stated in Polson, Scott and Windle (2013), Bayesian inference for logistic models using Pólya Gamma latent variables, Journal of the American Statistical Association 108, 1339 to 1349.
Status: proved.
Statement. For \(b>0\) and \(c\in\mathbb{R}\), the Pólya Gamma law \(PG(b,c)\) is the law of \(\omega=\frac{1}{2\pi^2}\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{g_k}{(k-\frac12)^2+c^2/(4\pi^2)}\), where \(g_1,g_2,\dots\) are independent Gamma variables with shape \(b\) and unit rate. Let \(p(\cdot\mid b,0)\) be the density of \(PG(b,0)\). Then for all \(b>0\), \(a\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(\psi\in\mathbb{R}\), \(\frac{(e^{\psi})^a}{(1+e^{\psi})^b}=2^{-b}e^{(a-b/2)\psi}\int_0^\infty e^{-\omega\psi^2/2}\,p(\omega\mid b,0)\,\mathrm{d}\omega\). Moreover, the conditional law of \(\omega\) given \(\psi\), that is the law with density proportional to \(e^{-\omega\psi^2/2}p(\omega\mid b,0)\) in \(\omega\), is \(PG(b,\psi)\).
Source: source/chapters/ch05_mixtures.tex, label thm:pg_identity.




Theorem 7.9, page 89 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. First stated in Carvalho, Polson and Scott (2010), The horseshoe estimator for sparse signals, Biometrika 97, 465 to 480.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \(\theta\mid\lambda\sim N(0,\lambda^2)\) with \(\lambda\) half Cauchy \(C^+(0,1)\) (the horseshoe prior with global scale \(\tau=1\)). The marginal density of \(\theta\) is \(p(\theta)=K\,e^{\theta^2/2}E_1(\theta^2/2)\), where \(K=1/\sqrt{2\pi^3}\) and \(E_1(x)=\int_x^\infty s^{-1}e^{-s}\,\mathrm{d}s\) is the exponential integral, and it satisfies, for all \(\theta\neq0\), \(\frac K2\log\big(1+\frac4{\theta^2}\big)<p(\theta)<K\log\big(1+\frac2{\theta^2}\big)\). In particular \(p\) has a logarithmic pole at zero and tails of order \(\theta^{-2}\).
Source: source/chapters/ext/ch05.tex, label thm:horseshoe_bounds.







Proposition 12.8, page 153 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \(\nu,T,L>0\). Let \(\mathbb{T}^2=(\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z})^2\), let \(\dot H^{s}_\diamond\) denote the Sobolev space of order \(s\) of divergence free, mean zero vector fields on \(\mathbb{T}^2\), and let \(f\in\dot H^{1}_\diamond\) be a forcing. Let \(\mathcal{X}=[0,T]\times\mathbb{T}^2\) with the uniform probability measure, and let \(e_1,e_2,\dots\) be the eigenfunctions of the Stokes operator on \(\mathbb{T}^2\), orthonormal in \(L^2\), with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\cdots\). For \(D\ge1\) and \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}^D\) let \(\mathcal{G}(\theta)(t,x)=u_\theta(t,x)\) be the velocity of the solution of the two dimensional Navier Stokes equations with viscosity \(\nu\), forcing \(f\) and initial condition \(\sum_{k\le D}\theta_ke_k\). Then there is a constant \(c>0\), depending only on \(\nu\), \(T\), \(\|f\|_{\dot H^{1}_\diamond}\), \(L\) and the torus, such that \(\big\|v^\top\nabla\mathcal{G}(\theta)\big\|_{L^2(\mathcal{X})}\ge c\,D^{-1/2}\,|v|\) for every \(D\ge1\), every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^D\) and every \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}^D\) with \(\big\|\sum_{k\le D}\theta_ke_k\big\|_{\dot H^{2}_\diamond}\le L\). Here \(v^\top\nabla\mathcal{G}(\theta)=\sum_{k\le D}v_k\,\partial\mathcal{G}(\theta)/\partial\theta_k\) is the derivative of \(\mathcal{G}\) at \(\theta\) in the direction \(v\) and \(|v|\) is the Euclidean norm.
Source: source/chapters/ext/ch10_nw.tex, label prop:gs_ns.




Proposition 12.10, page 157 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \(\Pi_n(\cdot\mid y)\) be posterior distributions of a parameter \(\theta\) given data \(y\), let \(L\) be a functional of the parameter, let \(\hat L_n\) be a statistic, and let \(H_n\) be a generator, a map that takes the data \(y\) and a uniform random variable \(U\) to a parameter value \(H_n(y,U)\). Write \(\tilde\Pi_n\) for the law of \(\sqrt n\,(L\theta-\hat L_n)\) when \(\theta\sim\Pi_n(\cdot\mid y)\), write \(\tilde G_n\) for the law of \(\sqrt n\,(L H_n(y,U)-\hat L_n)\) when \(U\) is uniform, and let \(d_{BL}\) be the bounded Lipschitz metric. Suppose that, in probability under the data generating law, \(d_{BL}\big(\tilde\Pi_n,N(0,\sigma^2)\big)\to0\) and \(d_{BL}\big(\tilde G_n,\tilde\Pi_n\big)\to0.\) Then \(d_{BL}\big(\tilde G_n,N(0,\sigma^2)\big)\to0\) in probability: the generated law satisfies the same Bernstein von Mises theorem as the posterior.
Source: source/chapters/ch10_ns_inference.tex, label prop:bvm_generators.







Lemma 14.3, page 189 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Work in the setting of Theorem 1 of Nickl (2024), the Bernstein von Mises theorem for forward trajectories: \(\Omega=[0,1]^d\) is the \(d\) dimensional torus with \(d\le3\), \(T>0\), \(f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})\), \(\theta_0\) is a smooth initial condition, \(u_\theta\) is the solution of \(\partial_tu-\Delta u=f(u)\), \(u(0)=\theta\), which is observed with standard normal noise at design points uniform on \([0,T]\times\Omega\), and \(\theta\) has the rescaled Gaussian series prior of Theorem 1 of Nickl (2024), of integer regularity \(\gamma>2+3d\). Let \(\mathbb{I}_{\theta_0}\) be the linearization of \(\theta\mapsto u_\theta\) at \(\theta_0\), \(\mathbb{I}_{\theta_0}^*\) its adjoint with respect to Lebesgue measure on \(\Omega\) and on \([0,T]\times\Omega\), and \(\mathcal{N}_{\theta_0}=N(0,T(\mathbb{I}_{\theta_0}^*\mathbb{I}_{\theta_0})^{-1})\) the Gaussian limit of the posterior of \(\theta\). Let \(0<t_{\min}<t_{\max}<\infty\), let \(\mathscr{C}=C([t_{\min},t_{\max}],C(\Omega))\) with the supremum norm, and let \(\mu\) be the law in \(\mathscr{C}\) of the solution \(U\) of \(\partial_tU-\Delta U-f'(u_{\theta_0})U=0\) with \(U(0)=\vartheta\sim\mathcal{N}_{\theta_0}\). Then the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of the Gaussian measure \(\mu\) is a nontrivial linear subspace of \(\mathscr{C}\), and \(r\mapsto\mu(\|U\|_{\mathscr{C}}\le r)\) is continuous and strictly increasing on \([0,\infty)\).
Source: source/chapters/ext/m1a.tex, label m:lem:nondeg.




Proposition 14.5, page 193 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Consider the heat equation \(\partial_tu=\nu\Delta u\) with viscosity \(\nu>0\) on the torus \(\mathbb{T}^d=[0,1]^d\), where \(\lambda_j\) are the eigenvalues of \(-\Delta\) (\(\lambda_j=4\pi^2|k_j|^2\) for the Fourier mode \(k_j\in\mathbb{Z}^d\setminus\{0\}\)), \(\lambda_1\) is the smallest, and \((e_j)\) is the corresponding orthonormal eigenbasis. There are \(N\) observations at design points uniform on \([0,T]\times\mathbb{T}^d\) with noise variance \(\varsigma^2\), the variance that the model normalizes to one and that is carried as a symbol only to show where it enters. In the constrained model the prior is placed on the initial condition, with independent Gaussian coefficients of variances \(\sigma_{0,j}^2=\rho^2(\lambda_j/\lambda_1)^{-\alpha}\), where \(\alpha>(d+1)/2\), so that the field is \(\sum_j\theta_je^{-\nu\lambda_jt}e_j\). In the unconstrained model, for comparison, the prior is a Gaussian process on the space time field \(u(t,x)\) with Fourier variances \(\sigma_{0,km}^2=\rho^2((\lambda_k+\omega_m^2)/\lambda_1)^{-\alpha}\), \(\omega_m=2\pi m/T\), \(m\in\mathbb{Z}\), where \(k\) runs over the spatial modes (those with \(\lambda_k\ge\lambda_1\)), so that the two priors have comparable regularity in \(x\). The Gram matrix of the design is replaced by its limit: \(\operatorname{diag}(\iota_j)\) with \(\iota_j=(1-e^{-2\nu\lambda_jT})/(2\nu\lambda_jT)\) in the constrained model, and the identity in the unconstrained one. Then: (i) the constrained posterior standard deviation of \(u(t,x)\) is \(\big(\sum_je^{-2\nu\lambda_jt}(N\iota_j/\varsigma^2+\sigma_{0,j}^{-2})^{-1}\big)^{1/2}\), decreasing in \(t\), and the effective number of parameters, \(\#\{j:N\iota_j\sigma_{0,j}^2\ge\varsigma^2\}\), is, for \(\varsigma=1\), of order \((N\rho^2/\nu T)^{d/(2\alpha+2)}\) as \(\Lambda=(N\rho^2\lambda_1^\alpha/(2\nu T))^{1/(\alpha+1)}\to\infty\) with \(\nu T\Lambda\geq1\), with constants that depend only on \(\alpha\), \(d\) and \(\rho\); (ii) the unconstrained posterior standard deviation is \(\big(\sum_{k,m}(N/\varsigma^2+\sigma_{0,km}^{-2})^{-1}\big)^{1/2}\), independent of \((t,x)\), and its effective number of parameters, \(\#\{(k,m):N\sigma_{0,km}^2\ge\varsigma^2\}\), is of order \(N^{(d+1)/(2\alpha)}\) as \(N\to\infty\); (iii) the ratio of the unconstrained to the constrained standard deviation at time \(t\) is at least \(e^{\nu\lambda_1t}\) times its value at \(t=0\), so it grows without bound as \(t\) increases, at the rate at which the manifold contracts.
Source: source/chapters/ext/m1a.tex, label m:prop:gain.







Lemma 15.1, page 206 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \((e_j)\) be an orthonormal basis of \(L^2(\Omega)\), let \(S_t\) be a strongly continuous semigroup on \(L^2(\Omega)\) with \(S_te_j=s_j(t)e_j\) and generator \(A\), let \((t_i,x_i)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\) and \(Y_i\in\mathbb{R}\) for \(i\le N\), let \(\Phi_{ij}=s_j(t_i)e_j(x_i)\) (\(i\le N\), \(j\le D\)) be the design matrix, so that \((\Phi^\top Y)_j=\sum_{i\le N}Y_is_j(t_i)e_j(x_i)\), and let \(r=\sum_{i\le N}Y_i\,\delta_{t_i}\otimes\delta_{x_i}\) be the empirical data measure on \([0,T]\times\Omega\). Then for every \(h=\sum_jh_je_j\in\operatorname{span}\{e_j:j\le D\}\), \(\langle\Phi^\top Y,h\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^D}=\sum_{i=1}^NY_i\,(S_{t_i}h)(x_i)=\big\langle h,\int_0^TS_t^*r(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\big\rangle\), so that \(\Phi^\top Y\) is the coefficient vector of \(w(0)\), where \(w\) is the mild solution of the backward problem \(-\partial_sw=A^*w+r\), \(w(T)=0\).
Source: source/chapters/ext/m2a.tex, label m:lem:adjoint.




Proposition 15.2, page 207 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Consider the linear model \(Y=\Phi\theta+\varepsilon\) with \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}^D\), design matrix \(\Phi_{ij}=s_j(t_i)e_j(x_i)\) (\(i\le N\), \(j\le D\), where \(S_te_j=s_j(t)e_j\) for a semigroup that is diagonal in the basis \((e_j)\)), noise \(\varepsilon\sim N(0,\mathrm{Id}_N)\) and Gaussian prior \(\theta\sim N(0,\Sigma_0)\). Let \(S_N=\Phi^\top Y\) be the adjoint statistic (the coefficient vector of \(w(0)\), where \(w\) solves the backward adjoint problem driven by the data) and \(V_N=(\Phi^\top\Phi+\Sigma_0^{-1})^{-1}\). Then \(S_N\) together with the design is sufficient for \(\theta\); the posterior given \(S_N\) is exactly the posterior given all the data, namely \(N(V_NS_N,V_N)\); and the conditional quantile map is exactly affine: for each coordinate \(j\) and \(\tau\in(0,1)\), \(Q_j(\tau\mid S_N)=(V_NS_N)_j+z_\tau(V_N)_{jj}^{1/2}\), where \(z_\tau\) is the \(\tau\) quantile of the standard normal law. The slope of this map in \(S_N\) is \(V_N\), not the identity. For the preconditioned summary \(\tilde S_N=V_NS_N\), which is the posterior mean, the map \(\tilde S_N\mapsto Q_j(\tau\mid S_N)\) has slope exactly one and, apart from the data independent scale term \(z_\tau(V_N)_{jj}^{1/2}\), intercept zero. Consequently generative Bayesian computation (GBC) with summary \(\tilde S_N\) and an identity plus scale generator is exact for every \(N\), up to the estimation of the \(D\times D\) scale from \(M\) simulations; in the linear model that scale is \(V_N\) itself and is known in closed form.
Source: source/chapters/ext/m2a.tex, label m:prop:linsuff.




Proposition 15.5, page 210 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \(\Omega=[0,1]^d\) be the torus, \(T>0\), \(\mathcal X=[0,T]\times\Omega\), and let \(\mathscr{G}(\theta)=u_\theta\) be the solution map of an evolution equation with initial condition \(\theta\) and values in \(W\). The data are \(Z^{(N)}=(Y_i,X_i)_{i\le N}\) with \(Y_i=\mathscr{G}(\theta)(X_i)+\varepsilon_i\), \(X_i\) i.i.d. uniform on \(\mathcal X\) and \(\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,I_W)\) independent. Let \((e_j)\) be the orthonormal Laplace eigenbasis of mean zero functions, with eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\asymp j^{2/d}\); let the prior \(\Pi\) be the law of \((\sqrt N\delta_N)^{-1}\sum_j\lambda_j^{-\gamma/2}g_je_j\) with \(g_j\) i.i.d. \(N(0,1)\) and \(\delta_N=N^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}\), and \(\Pi_N=\Pi(\cdot\mid Z^{(N)})\) the posterior; let \(\theta_0\) be the true initial condition, \(P^N_{\theta_0}\) the law of the data, \(\mathbb{I}_\vartheta\) the linearization of \(\mathscr{G}\) at \(\vartheta\), \(\mathcal{N}_\vartheta=N(0,T(\mathbb{I}_\vartheta^*\mathbb{I}_\vartheta)^{-1})\), \(J_N\asymp N\delta_N^2\) and \(p_N\) the projection onto \(\operatorname{span}\{e_j:j\le J_N\}\).
Suppose Conditions 1 and 2 of Nickl (2024) hold with integer \(\gamma>\max(3\zeta+3d/2+2,\eta_0)\) and \(k>\max(\zeta+5d/2,\eta_0)\) as in his Bernstein von Mises theorem (\(\eta_0\) the index of his invertibility condition), that is, the prior above with Sobolev reproducing kernel space \(H^\gamma\) and, for the forward map on balls of \(H^{\bar\gamma}\), uniform \(L^\infty\) bounds, \(L^2\) Lipschitz continuity, a linearization at \(\theta_0\) with quadratic remainder, \(L^\infty\) mapping properties from \(H^\zeta\) with \(\zeta>d/2\), the stability estimate \(\|\mathscr{G}(\theta)-\mathscr{G}(\theta_0)\|_{L^2(\mathcal X)}\ge c\|\theta-\theta_0\|_{H^{-1}}\) and an invertible information operator (\(\bar\gamma\) is the Sobolev index of the localization ball, \(\max(2,2\zeta)<\bar\gamma<\gamma-\max(1,d/2)\)). Let \(\kappa\) satisfy \(2d+\zeta<\kappa<k-d/2\).
The one step efficient score summary is defined by cross fitting. The sample is split into two halves with index sets \(\mathcal I_1,\mathcal I_2\) of sizes differing by at most one. For \(b=1,2\) a preliminary estimate \(\bar\theta^{[b]}_N\) is computed from half \(b\) alone, takes values in the parameter space and satisfies \(\|\bar\theta^{[b]}_N-\theta_0\|_{H^\xi}=O_P(\tilde\delta_N(\xi))\) for \(0\le\xi\le\bar\gamma\), where \(\tilde\delta_N(\xi)=\delta_N^{(\bar\gamma-\xi)/(\bar\gamma+1)}\). With \(\bar e_j^{\,\vartheta}=T(\mathbb{I}_\vartheta^*\mathbb{I}_\vartheta)^{-1}e_j\), put for \(j\le J_N\) \(S_{N,j}=\frac12\sum_{b=1,2}\big[\langle e_j,\bar\theta^{[b]}_N\rangle+\frac1{|\mathcal I_{3-b}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{3-b}}\langle\mathbb{I}_{\bar\theta^{[b]}_N}p_N(\bar e_j^{\,\bar\theta^{[b]}_N})(X_i),\,Y_i-u_{\bar\theta^{[b]}_N}(X_i)\rangle_W\big]\) and \(\hat S^{J_N}_N=\sum_{j\le J_N}S_{N,j}e_j\). The efficient centering of Nickl’s proof is \(\hat\theta_N=\sum_{j\ge1}\hat\Psi_{N,j}e_j\) with \(\hat\Psi_{N,j}=\langle e_j,\theta_0\rangle+\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\langle\mathbb{I}_{\theta_0}p_N(\bar e_j^{\,\theta_0})(X_i),\varepsilon_i\rangle_W\).
Suppose further that \(\sqrt N\,\tilde\delta_N(0)\tilde\delta_N(\zeta)\to0\); that \(\gamma<(\bar\gamma+1)(\kappa-d/2)\) unless \(\mathbb{I}^*_{\theta_0}\mathbb{I}_{\theta_0}\) is diagonal in \((e_j)\) or the preliminary estimates converge at the rate \(\delta_N\) in \(H^{-1}\); and that the weights depend on the linearization point in a Lipschitz way: for every \(B>0\) there is \(L=L(B)\) such that for all \(\vartheta\) with \(\|\vartheta\|_{H^{\bar\gamma}}\le B\) and all \(j\le J_N\), \(\|\mathbb{I}_\vartheta p_N(\bar e_j^{\,\vartheta})-\mathbb{I}_{\theta_0}p_N(\bar e_j^{\,\theta_0})\|_{L^2(\mathcal X)}\le L\,\|\vartheta-\theta_0\|_{H^\zeta}\|e_j\|_{H^{\kappa+2}}\). Then \(\sqrt N\,\|\hat S^{J_N}_N-\hat\theta_N\|_{H^{-k-2}}\to0\) in \(P^N_{\theta_0}\) probability, and consequently \(\mathscr{W}_1\big(\operatorname{Law}(\sqrt N(\theta-\hat S^{J_N}_N)\mid Z^{(N)}),\mathcal{N}_{\theta_0}\big)\to0\) in \(P^N_{\theta_0}\) probability, where \(\mathscr{W}_1\) is the Wasserstein distance of order one on \(H^{-k-2}\).
Source: source/chapters/ext/m2a.tex, label m:prop:suff.




Proposition 15.6, page 213 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. In Nickl’s framework, for the cross fitted one step efficient score summary of the book (torus \(\Omega=[0,1]^d\), data \(Y_i=\mathscr{G}(\theta_0)(X_i)+\varepsilon_i\) at the true initial condition \(\theta_0\) with \(X_i\) i.i.d. uniform on \(\mathcal X=[0,T]\times\Omega\) and \(\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,I_W)\), orthonormal Laplace eigenbasis \((e_j)\) with eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\asymp j^{2/d}\), rescaled Gaussian series prior with exponent \(\gamma\) and \(\delta_N=N^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}\), \(J_N\asymp N\delta_N^2\), \(p_N\) the projection onto the first \(J_N\) modes, \(\mathbb{I}_\vartheta\) the linearization of \(\mathscr{G}\) at \(\vartheta\), \(\tilde\delta_N(\xi)=\delta_N^{(\bar\gamma-\xi)/(\bar\gamma+1)}\)), suppose that Conditions 1 and 2 of Nickl (2024) hold (the prior and, for the forward map on balls of \(H^{\bar\gamma}\), uniform bounds, a linearization at \(\theta_0\) with quadratic remainder, the stability estimate \(\|\mathscr{G}(\theta)-\mathscr{G}(\theta_0)\|_{L^2(\mathcal X)}\ge c\|\theta-\theta_0\|_{H^{-1}}\) and an invertible information operator). Suppose that for every \(B>0\) there are constants \(0<c_B\le C_B<\infty\) such that for every \(\vartheta\) in the parameter space with \(\|\vartheta\|_{H^{\bar\gamma}}\le B\), \(c_B\|h\|_{H^{-1}}\le\|\mathbb{I}_\vartheta h\|_{L^2(\mathcal X)}\le C_B\|h\|_{H^{-1}}\) for all \(h\in L^2_0(\Omega)\) (with \(\dot H^{-1}_\diamond\) and \(\dot H_\diamond\) in place of \(H^{-1}\) and \(L^2_0(\Omega)\) for the Stokes and Navier Stokes equations), and that the preliminary estimates \(\bar\theta^{[b]}_N\) of the cross fitted one step summary (each computed from one half sample alone, with values in the parameter space and \(\|\bar\theta^{[b]}_N-\theta_0\|_{H^\xi}=O_P(\tilde\delta_N(\xi))\) for \(0\le\xi\le\bar\gamma\)) satisfy \(\|\bar\theta^{[b]}_N-\theta_0\|_{H^{-1}}=O_P(\delta_N)\) for \(b=1,2\). Then the projected one step statistic \(\hat S^{J_N}_N\) satisfies \(\|\hat S^{J_N}_N-\theta_0\|_{H^s}=O_P\big(N^{(s+1-\gamma)/(2\gamma+d)}\big)\) for every \(-1\le s\le\gamma\). If moreover \(\bar\gamma<\gamma-1\), then \(\|\hat S^{J_N}_N-\theta_0\|_{L^2}=o_P(\tilde\delta_N(0))\) and \(\|\hat S^{J_N}_N-\theta_0\|_{H^{\bar\gamma}}=o_P(1)\). For a linear forward map whose information operator is diagonal in \((e_j)\), as for the heat and Stokes equations, the same conclusions hold without the rate in \(H^{-1}\).

Lemma 15.11, page 219 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.

Proposition 15.12, page 219 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.

Proposition 15.13, page 220 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \(\mathscr{G}\) be the solution map of the heat equation \(\partial_tu=\nu\Delta u\) on \(\mathbb{T}^d\), with \(W=\mathbb{R}\), or of the Stokes equations on \(\mathbb{T}^2\), with \(W=\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(d=2\), and let \((e_j)\) be a real orthonormal eigenbasis of the mean zero functions, respectively of the divergence free mean zero fields, with \(\sup_x|e_j(x)|_W\le\sqrt2\), as for the trigonometric basis; thus \(s_j(t)=e^{-\nu\lambda_jt}\) and \(\lambda_j\asymp j^{2/d}\). The data are \(Z^{(N)}=(Y_i,X_i)_{i\le N}\) with \(Y_i=\mathscr{G}(\theta_0)(X_i)+\varepsilon_i\), \(X_i=(t_i,x_i)\) i.i.d. uniform on \([0,T]\times\mathbb{T}^d\) and \(\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,I_W)\), where \(\theta_0\in H^\gamma\) lies in the closed span of \((e_j)\) and \(\gamma>d+1\) is the exponent of the prior \(\Pi\), the law of \((\sqrt N\delta_N)^{-1}\sum_j\lambda_j^{-\gamma/2}g_je_j\) with \(g_j\) i.i.d. \(N(0,1)\) and \(\delta_N=N^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}\); let \(k>d/2\), \(J_N\asymp N\delta_N^2\) and \(\iota_j=\frac1T\int_0^Ts_j(t)^2\,\mathrm{d}t\). Retain \(D=D_N\) modes and give their coefficients the truncation of the prior, \(N(0,\Sigma_0)\) with \(\Sigma_0=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{0,j}^2)_{j\le D}\) and \(\sigma_{0,j}^2=\lambda_j^{-\gamma}/(N\delta_N^2)\); write \(\Pi^D(\cdot\mid Z^{(N)})\) for the resulting posterior and \(\Phi\) for the \(N\times D\) design matrix with entries \(s_j(t_i)e_j(x_i)\) (a pair of rows per observation for Stokes). Suppose that \(D_N\to\infty\), \(\delta_N^2D_N^{2+2/d}\to0\) and \(ND_N^{-2(k+2+\gamma)/d}\to0\), which holds for \(D_N\asymp J_N\). Let \(\hat S^{\rm reg}_N\) be the regularized one step summary computed on the \(D\) retained modes from a pilot \(\bar\theta_N\) in their span, which may depend on the data in any way: \(\hat S^{\rm reg}_N=\bar\theta_N+(F_N+\Sigma_0^{-1})^{-1}\big(\Phi^\top(Y-\Phi\bar\theta_N)-\Sigma_0^{-1}\bar\theta_N\big)\) with \(F_N=\Phi^\top\Phi\), which equals \((\Phi^\top\Phi+\Sigma_0^{-1})^{-1}\Phi^\top Y\), the posterior mean under the truncated prior, for every pilot. Let \(\hat\theta_N=\theta_0+\sum_{j\le J_N}\xi_je_j\) with \(\xi_j=(N\iota_j)^{-1}\sum_{i\le N}s_j(t_i)\langle e_j(x_i),\varepsilon_i\rangle_W\) be the efficient centering of Nickl (2024) for these equations, \(\mathcal{N}_{\theta_0}\) the Gaussian law with covariance \(\operatorname{diag}(1/\iota_j)\) in the basis \((e_j)\), and \(\mathscr{W}_1\) the Wasserstein distance of order one on \(H^{-k-2}\). Then, in \(P^N_{\theta_0}\) probability where convergence in probability is meant:

\(\sqrt N\|\hat S^{\rm reg}_N-\hat\theta_N\|_{H^{-k-2}}\to0\) in probability; (ii) \(\mathscr{W}_1\big(\operatorname{Law}(\sqrt N(\theta-\hat S^{\rm reg}_N)\mid Z^{(N)}),\mathcal{N}_{\theta_0}\big)\to0\) in probability for \(\theta\sim\Pi^D(\cdot\mid Z^{(N)})\); (iii) \(\sqrt N(\hat S^{\rm reg}_N-\theta_0)\to\mathcal{N}_{\theta_0}\) in distribution in \(H^{-k-2}\); (iv) for the heat equation with integer \(\gamma>3d+2\) and \(k>3d\), Nickl’s Bernstein von Mises theorem applies, (ii) holds also for \(\theta\) drawn from the posterior \(\Pi_N\) under the untruncated prior, and the mean \(\tilde\theta_N\) of \(\Pi_N\) satisfies \(\sqrt N\|\hat S^{\rm reg}_N-\tilde\theta_N\|_{H^{-k-2}}\to0\) in probability; (v) for the heat equation, whenever the hypotheses of the equivalence of the cross fitted one step summary \(\hat S^{J_N}_N\) with the efficient centering hold (catalog entry equivalence_with_the_efficient_centering), \(\sqrt N\|\hat S^{\rm reg}_N-\hat S^{J_N}_N\|_{H^{-k-2}}\to0\) in probability.

Proposition 15.14, page 225 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let the setting be that of the regularized summary on \(D=D_N\) modes for the heat equation \(\partial_tu=\nu\Delta u\) on \(\mathbb{T}^d\) (\(W=\mathbb{R}\)) or the Stokes equations on \(\mathbb{T}^2\) (\(W=\mathbb{R}^2\), \(d=2\)): \((e_j)\) a real orthonormal eigenbasis of the mean zero functions, respectively divergence free mean zero fields, with \(\sup_x|e_j(x)|_W\le\sqrt2\); \(s_j(t)=e^{-\nu\lambda_jt}\); data \(Y_i=\mathscr{G}(\theta_0)(X_i)+\varepsilon_i\) with \(X_i\) i.i.d. uniform on \([0,T]\times\mathbb{T}^d\) and \(\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,I_W)\); \(\iota_j=\frac1T\int_0^Ts_j(t)^2\,\mathrm{d}t\); \(\hat S^{\rm reg}_N=(\Phi^\top\Phi+\Sigma_0^{-1})^{-1}\Phi^\top Y\) the regularized summary (posterior mean under the truncated prior) with \(\Phi_{ij}=s_j(t_i)e_j(x_i)\); \(\hat\theta_N=\theta_0+\sum_{j\le J_N}\xi_je_j\) with \(\xi_j=(N\iota_j)^{-1}\sum_is_j(t_i)\langle e_j(x_i),\varepsilon_i\rangle_W\) the efficient centering; \(\mathscr{W}_1\) the Wasserstein distance of order one on \(H^{-k-2}\); \(\mathcal{N}_{\theta_0}\) the Gaussian law with covariance \(\operatorname{diag}(1/\iota_j)\). Take now \(\theta_0\in H^\beta\) in the closed span of \((e_j)\) with \(\beta>d/2\), \(k>d/2-1\), and give the \(D=D_N\) retained coefficients the fixed prior \(\sigma_{0,j}^2=\rho^2\lambda_j^{-\alpha}\) with \(\rho>0\) and \(\alpha>d/2\) (not rescaled with \(N\)). Suppose that \(\beta\ge\alpha-k-1\), that \(D_N\to\infty\) with \(\sup_NND_N^{-2(k+2+\beta)/d}<\infty\) (a condition void when \(\theta_0\) has finitely many nonzero coefficients), and that \(\alpha>d\) or \(D_N^{2+2/d}/N\to0\), and form the centering \(\hat\theta_N\) with the first \(J_N\) modes, for any \(J_N\to\infty\). Then (i) \(\sqrt N\|\hat S^{\rm reg}_N-\hat\theta_N\|_{H^{-k-2}}\to0\) in probability, (ii) \(\mathscr{W}_1(\operatorname{Law}(\sqrt N(\theta-\hat S^{\rm reg}_N)\mid Z^{(N)}),\mathcal{N}_{\theta_0})\to0\) in probability for \(\theta\) drawn from the posterior under the truncated prior, (iii) \(\sqrt N(\hat S^{\rm reg}_N-\theta_0)\to\mathcal{N}_{\theta_0}\) in distribution in \(H^{-k-2}\), and (v) for the heat equation, \(\sqrt N\|\hat S^{\rm reg}_N-\hat S^{J_N}_N\|_{H^{-k-2}}\to0\) in probability whenever the hypotheses of the equivalence of the cross fitted one step summary \(\hat S^{J_N}_N\) with the efficient centering hold. If \(\alpha>d\), (i) to (iii) hold also for \(D=\infty\), that is, under the untruncated prior.
For the rescaled prior \(\sigma_{0,j}^2=\lambda_j^{-\gamma}/(N\delta_N^2)\), \(\delta_N=N^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}\), \(\gamma>d+1\), of the regularized summary on \(J_N\) modes (catalog entry the_regularized_summary_on_modes_heat_and_stokes), the conclusions of that statement hold without its condition \(\delta_N^2D_N^{2+2/d}\to0\), and its claims (i) to (iii) hold also for \(D=\infty\), that is, for the posterior \(\Pi_N\) under the untruncated rescaled prior and its mean \(\tilde\theta_N\). Hence the last two claims of its part (iv) (that (ii) holds for \(\theta\) drawn from \(\Pi_N\) and that \(\sqrt N\|\hat S^{\rm reg}_N-\tilde\theta_N\|_{H^{-k-2}}\to0\) in probability) hold for the Stokes equations as well, and for the heat equation without its restrictions on \(\gamma\) and \(k\); and when \(\theta_0\) meets both sets of hypotheses, the regularized summaries under the two priors, and if \(\alpha>d\) the untruncated posterior means, are \(\sqrt N\) equivalent in \(H^{-k-2}\).

Proposition 15.16, page 228 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Consider the reaction diffusion equation \(\partial_tu-\Delta u=f(u)\), \(u(0)=\theta\), on the torus \(\Omega=[0,1]^d\) with \(f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})\) and \(d\le3\) (the class of Theorem 1 of Nickl (2024)), with the rescaled Gaussian series prior \(\Pi\) of integer exponent \(\gamma>2+3d\) (\(\delta_N=N^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}\), \(J_N\asymp N\delta_N^2\)), smooth true initial condition \(\theta_0\), parameter space \(H^{\bar\gamma}\) with \(\bar\gamma>3+d/2\), and let \(k>3d\), so that Theorem 5 of Nickl (2024) gives Conditions 1 and 2 with \(\gamma\) and \(k\) as in his Bernstein von Mises theorem. Retain \(D=J_N\) modes with the truncated prior \(\Sigma_0=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{0,j}^2)_{j\le J_N}\), \(\sigma_{0,j}^2=\lambda_j^{-\gamma}/(N\delta_N^2)\). The sample is split into halves with index sets \(\mathcal I_1,\mathcal I_2\); let the preliminary estimates \(\bar\theta^{[b]}_N\) (computed from half \(b\), with the rates of the cross fitted one step summary) lie in the span of \(e_1,\dots,e_{J_N}\), as their projections do with the same rates. For \(b=1,2\) let \(\hat S^{{\rm reg},b}_N=\bar\theta^{[b]}_N+(F^b_N+\Sigma_0^{-1})^{-1}\big(\mathbb{I}^*_{\bar\theta^{[b]}_N}[\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{3-b}}r_i\,\delta_{X_i}]-\Sigma_0^{-1}\bar\theta^{[b]}_N\big)\) with residuals \(r_i=Y_i-u_{\bar\theta^{[b]}_N}(X_i)\) and \(F^b_N\) the realized information \(\mathbb{I}^*_{\bar\theta^{[b]}_N}\mathbb{I}_{\bar\theta^{[b]}_N}\) on the design points \(X_i\), \(i\in\mathcal I_{3-b}\), compressed to the retained modes, and put \(\hat S^{\rm reg}_N=\frac12(\hat S^{{\rm reg},1}_N+\hat S^{{\rm reg},2}_N)\). Let \(\hat\theta_N\) be the efficient centering of Nickl’s proof, \(\mathcal{N}_{\theta_0}=N(0,T(\mathbb{I}_{\theta_0}^*\mathbb{I}_{\theta_0})^{-1})\), \(\Pi_N\) the posterior, \(\tilde\theta_N\) its mean and \(\mathscr{W}_1\) the Wasserstein distance of order one on \(H^{-k-2}\). Then, in \(P^N_{\theta_0}\) probability: (i) \(\sqrt N\|\hat S^{\rm reg}_N-\hat\theta_N\|_{H^{-k-2}}\to0\); (ii) \(\mathscr{W}_1(\operatorname{Law}(\sqrt N(\theta-\hat S^{\rm reg}_N)\mid Z^{(N)}),\mathcal{N}_{\theta_0})\to0\) for \(\theta\sim\Pi_N\), the mean \(\tilde\theta_N\) satisfies \(\sqrt N\|\hat S^{\rm reg}_N-\tilde\theta_N\|_{H^{-k-2}}\to0\), and \(\sqrt N(\hat S^{\rm reg}_N-\theta_0)\to\mathcal{N}_{\theta_0}\) in distribution in \(H^{-k-2}\); (iii) under the hypotheses of the equivalence of the cross fitted one step summary \(\hat S^{J_N}_N\) with the efficient centering other than the Lipschitz condition on the weights (which the information operator lemma for this class supplies), \(\sqrt N\|\hat S^{\rm reg}_N-\hat S^{J_N}_N\|_{H^{-k-2}}\to0\).

Proposition 15.18, page 231 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. For the heat or the Stokes equation on the torus, with semigroup eigenvalues \(s_j(t)=e^{-\nu\lambda_jt}\) in the Laplace eigenbasis \((e_j)\) (\(\lambda_j\asymp j^{2/d}\)), data \(Y_i=\mathscr{G}(\theta)(X_i)+\varepsilon_i\) with \(X_i\) i.i.d. uniform on \([0,T]\times\Omega\) and \(\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,I_W)\), and per mode information \(\iota_j=\frac1T\int_0^Ts_j(t)^2\,\mathrm{d}t\), consider the first \(J\) modes with prior \(\Pi^J=N(0,\Sigma_0)\), \(\Sigma_0=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{0,j}^2)_{j\le J}\), in the Gaussian experiment that observes \(\theta_j+(N\iota_j)^{-1/2}\xi_j\), \(j\le J\), with independent standard normal \(\xi_j\). Its information matrix is \(\operatorname{diag}(N\iota_j)\), the population value of the Gram matrix \(\Phi^\top\Phi\) of the design, and it is the \(J\) mode experiment of the Bernstein von Mises limit, whose covariance is \(T(\mathbb{I}^*\mathbb{I})^{-1}/N=\operatorname{diag}(1/(N\iota_j))\), where \(\mathbb{I}\) is the forward map of the equation, which is linear. Write \(\kappa_j=N\iota_j\sigma_{0,j}^2\) for the per mode ratio of information to prior precision, and let \(I_N=\mathbb{E}^\Pi\big[\log\frac{\mathrm{d}\Pi^J(\cdot\mid Z^{(N)})}{\mathrm{d}\Pi^J}\,\big|\,Z^{(N)}\big]\) be the realized information gain, with \(\Pi^J(\cdot\mid Z^{(N)})\) the posterior and \(\tilde\theta^J_N\) the posterior mean. Then for every \(N\) and \(J\), \(I_N=\frac12\sum_{j\le J}\big[\log(1+\kappa_j)-\frac{\kappa_j}{1+\kappa_j}\big]+\frac12\tilde\theta_N^{J\top}\Sigma_0^{-1}\tilde\theta^J_N\), and averaging over the prior predictive law gives the Lindley expected information gain \(\mathbf{E}\,I_N=\frac12\log\det\big(\mathrm{Id}+\frac NT\mathbb{I}^*\mathbb{I}\,\Sigma_0\big)=\frac12\sum_{j\le J}\log(1+\kappa_j)\). In the linear model with \(D=J\) modes, that is, with the realized information \(\Phi^\top\Phi\) in place of \(\operatorname{diag}(N\iota_j)\), both identities hold conditionally on the design, with the \(\kappa_j\) replaced by the eigenvalues of \(\Sigma_0^{1/2}\Phi^\top\Phi\,\Sigma_0^{1/2}\). Every mode contributes the strictly positive amount \(\frac12\log(1+\kappa_j)\), and every mode has posterior variance \(\sigma_{0,j}^2/(1+\kappa_j)\) strictly below its prior variance; the modes with \(\kappa_j>1\) are those whose posterior variance falls below half the prior variance. Under the rescaled prior \(\sigma_{0,j}^2=\lambda_j^{-\gamma}/(N\delta_N^2)\) with \(\delta_N=N^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}\) and \(J=J_N\asymp N\delta_N^2\), the number of these is \(J^{\rm eff}_N=\#\{j\le J_N:\kappa_j>1\}\asymp N^{\gamma d/((\gamma+1)(2\gamma+d))}=J_N^{\gamma/(\gamma+1)}=o(J_N)\), so the experiment is informative in every retained mode, but strongly informative in only a vanishing fraction of them.

Lemma 15.21, page 233 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \(\mathscr{G}\) be a measurable forward map in the model \(Y_i=\mathscr{G}(\theta)(X_i)+\varepsilon_i\) (design \(X_i\) i.i.d. uniform on \(\mathcal X=[0,T]\times\Omega\), noise \(\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,I_W)\)), and let the prior be a centered Gaussian measure under which the coordinates \(\langle\theta,e_j\rangle\) in an orthonormal basis \((e_j)\) are independent with variances \(\sigma_{0,j}^2>0\). For a number \(J\) of modes let \(\theta^J=(\langle\theta,e_j\rangle)_{j\le J}\), let \(\Pi^J\) and \(\Pi^J(\cdot\mid Z^{(N)})\) be its prior and posterior laws, \(\Sigma^J_0=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{0,j}^2)_{j\le J}\), \(m_N\) and \(V_N\) the posterior mean and covariance of \(\theta^J\), \(I_N=\mathrm{KL}\big(\Pi^J(\cdot\mid Z^{(N)})\,\|\,\Pi^J\big)\) the realized information gain, \(\mathbf{P}\) the prior predictive law (parameter \(\vartheta\sim\Pi\), then data \(Z^{(N)}\sim P^N_\vartheta\)) and \(\mathbf{E}\) its expectation. Then for every \(N\) and \(J\): (i) almost surely \(I_N=\mathrm{KL}\big(N(m_N,V_N)\,\|\,\Pi^J\big)+\Gamma_N\), where \(\Gamma_N=\mathrm{KL}\big(\Pi^J(\cdot\mid Z^{(N)})\,\|\,N(m_N,V_N)\big)\ge0\), and \(\Gamma_N\le\mathrm{KL}\big(\Pi^J(\cdot\mid Z^{(N)})\,\|\,G\big)\) for every nondegenerate Gaussian law \(G\) on \(\mathbb{R}^J\); (ii) if \(\int\|\mathscr{G}(\vartheta)\|^2_{L^\infty(\mathcal X)}\,\mathrm{d}\Pi(\vartheta)<\infty\), then \(\mathbf{E}\,I_N=I(\theta^J;Z^{(N)})<\infty\) (the mutual information) and \(\mathbf{E}\,I_N=\frac12\,\mathbf{E}\log\det\big(\Sigma^J_0V_N^{-1}\big)+\mathbf{E}\,\Gamma_N\). In the linear Gaussian models of the heat and Stokes equations the posterior is \(N(m_N,V)\) with \(V\) not depending on the data, so \(\Gamma_N=0\) and (i) and (ii) reduce to the two displays of the expected utility form of the Bernstein von Mises limit.

Theorem 15.22, page 234 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.

Statement. Corollary 15.23, page 236 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Proposition 15.24, page 236 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Proposition 15.25, page 238 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \(\mathscr{G}\) be a measurable forward map in the model \(Y_i=\mathscr{G}(\theta)(X_i)+\varepsilon_i\) (\(X_i\) i.i.d. uniform on \(\mathcal X=[0,T]\times\Omega\), \(\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,I_W)\)), let the prior \(\Pi\) be a centered Gaussian measure under which the coordinates \(\langle\theta,e_j\rangle\) are independent with variances \(\sigma_{0,j}^2>0\), and assume \(\int\|\mathscr{G}(\vartheta)\|^2_{L^\infty(\mathcal X)}\,\mathrm{d}\Pi(\vartheta)<\infty\). Fix the number of modes \(J\), let \(\theta^J=(\langle\theta,e_j\rangle)_{j\le J}\), \(\Sigma^J_0=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{0,j}^2)_{j\le J}\), \(I_N=\mathrm{KL}(\Pi^J(\cdot\mid Z^{(N)})\,\|\,\Pi^J)\) the realized information gain, \(\mathbf{E}\) the expectation under the prior predictive law, and \(\mathcal J^J_N(\vartheta)=\frac NT\big(\langle\mathbb{I}_\vartheta e_j,\mathbb{I}_\vartheta e_{j'}\rangle_{L^2(\mathcal X)}\big)_{j,j'\le J}\) the \(J\) block of the Fisher information of \(N\) observations at \(\vartheta\), with \(\mathbb{I}_\vartheta\) the linearization of \(\mathscr{G}\) at \(\vartheta\). Assume that for \(\Pi\) almost every \(\eta\) in the closed span of \((e_j)_{j>J}\) the map \(x\mapsto\mathscr{G}(\eta+\sum_{j\le J}x_je_j)\) from \(\mathbb{R}^J\) into \(C(\mathcal X)\) is continuously differentiable, with partial derivatives \(\mathbb{I}_\vartheta e_j\) at \(\vartheta=\eta+\sum_{j\le J}x_je_j\). If \(\bar{\mathcal J}^J_N=\int\mathcal J^J_N(\vartheta)\,\mathrm{d}\Pi(\vartheta)\) is finite, then for every \(N\), \(\mathbf{E}\,I_N=I(\theta^J;Z^{(N)})\le\frac12\log\det\big(\mathrm{Id}+(\Sigma^J_0)^{1/2}\,\bar{\mathcal J}^J_N\,(\Sigma^J_0)^{1/2}\big)\). If moreover the prior is the rescaled Gaussian series prior with exponent \(\gamma>d\), and the matrix \(\mathcal J^J_N(\vartheta)/N\), which does not depend on \(N\), is continuous at \(\vartheta=0\) for the supremum norm, bounded by a polynomial in \(\|\vartheta\|_\infty\), and invertible at \(\vartheta=0\), then for fixed \(J\), \(\mathbf{E}\,I_N\le\frac12\log\det\big(\mathrm{Id}+(\Sigma^J_0)^{1/2}\,\mathcal J^J_N(0)\,(\Sigma^J_0)^{1/2}\big)+o(1)\).

Proposition 15.26, page 239 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \(\partial_tu=\Delta u+f(u)\), \(u(0)=\theta\), on the torus \(\Omega=[0,1]^d\) with \(f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})\) and \(d\le3\), observed as in the model \(Y_i=\mathscr{G}(\theta)(X_i)+\varepsilon_i\) with \(X_i\) i.i.d. uniform on \(\mathcal X=[0,T]\times\Omega\) and \(\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,1)\); let \((e_j)\) be the real trigonometric basis, of the functions \(\sqrt2\cos(2\pi k\cdot x)\) and \(\sqrt2\sin(2\pi k\cdot x)\) with eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\); let the prior \(\Pi\) be the rescaled Gaussian series prior with exponent \(\gamma>d\) and variances \(\sigma_{0,j}^2=\lambda_j^{-\gamma}/(N\delta_N^2)\), \(\delta_N=N^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}\); and let the number of modes \(J\) be fixed. Let \(I_N\) be the realized information gain for the first \(J\) modes and \(\mathbf{E}\) the expectation under the prior predictive law. Let \(v\) solve \(v'=f(v)\), \(v(0)=0\), \(\chi(t)=\int_0^tf'(v(s))\,\mathrm{d}s\), \(\iota^0_j=\frac1T\int_0^Te^{2\chi(t)-2\lambda_jt}\,\mathrm{d}t\) and \(\kappa^0_j=N\iota^0_j\sigma_{0,j}^2\) (the information at the center of the prior). Then: (i) \(\mathbf{E}\,I_N\le\frac12\sum_{j\le J}\log(1+\kappa^0_j)+o(1)\). (ii) If \(f\) vanishes on \([-a,a]\) for some \(a>0\), then \(\iota^0_j=\iota_j=(1-e^{-2\lambda_jT})/(2\lambda_jT)\), the value for the heat equation with \(\nu=1\), and \(\mathbf{E}\,I_N=\frac12\sum_{j\le J}\log(1+\kappa^0_j)+o(1)\). (iii) Let \(d\ge2\) and let \(f\) be as in (ii), with moreover \(f\ge0\), \(f\) nondecreasing on \((-\infty,b]\) and strictly increasing on \((a,b)\) for some \(b>a\). The first mode \(e_1\), with \(\lambda_1=4\pi^2\), is \(\sqrt2\cos(2\pi x_p)\) or \(\sqrt2\sin(2\pi x_p)\) for some coordinate \(p\); let \(\theta_0(x)=A\cos(2\pi x_q)\) with \(q\ne p\) and \(a<A<b\), and let \(T\) be so small that the solution of \(w'=f(w)\), \(w(0)=A\), stays at most \(b\) on \([0,T]\). Then \(\|\mathbb{I}_{\theta_0}e_1\|^2_{L^2(\mathcal X)}>T\iota_1\), and for \(J=1\), writing \(\mathcal J^1_N(\theta_0)=\frac NT\|\mathbb{I}_{\theta_0}e_1\|^2_{L^2(\mathcal X)}\) for the Fisher information at \(\theta_0\), \(\frac12\log\big(1+\sigma^2_{0,1}\mathcal J^1_N(\theta_0)\big)-\mathbf{E}\,I_N\to\frac12\log\frac{\|\mathbb{I}_{\theta_0}e_1\|^2_{L^2(\mathcal X)}}{T\iota_1}>0\). (iv) Under the hypotheses of (iii), let \(\psi(r)=(1-e^{-2\lambda_1r})/(2\lambda_1)\), let \(\psi(T-t)f'(u_{\theta_0}(t,x))<2\) for \((t,x)\in\mathcal X\) (as when \(T\sup f'<2\)), and let \(\lambda_j=\lambda_1\) for \(j\le J\). Then \(\Sigma_J(0)-\Sigma_J(\theta_0)\) is positive definite, where \(\Sigma_J(\vartheta)=\big(T\langle e_j,(\mathbb{I}^*_\vartheta\mathbb{I}_\vartheta)^{-1}e_{j'}\rangle\big)_{j,j'\le J}\) is the covariance of the Bernstein von Mises limit in the first \(J\) modes and \(\Sigma_J(0)=\mathrm{Id}/\iota_1\), and \(\frac12\log\det\big(\mathrm{Id}+N\sigma^2_{0,1}\Sigma_J(\theta_0)^{-1}\big)-\mathbf{E}\,I_N\to\frac12\log\det\big(\Sigma_J(0)\Sigma_J(\theta_0)^{-1}\big)>0\).

Proposition 15.28, page 243 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. In the linear model \(Y=\Phi\theta+\varepsilon\) with design matrix \(\Phi_{ij}=s_j(t_i)e_j(x_i)\) and unknown noise variance \(\varsigma^2\) (\(\varepsilon\sim N(0,\varsigma^2\mathrm{Id}_N)\)), conditionally on the design the pair \(\big(\Phi^\top Y,\ \|Y\|^2\big)\) is sufficient for \((\theta,\varsigma^2)\), and the conditional law of \(\theta\) given the pair and \(\varsigma^2\) depends on the data only through \(\Phi^\top Y\). If instead the observation noise is replaced by an observed diffusion path on \([0,T]\) with unknown diffusion coefficient, \(\mathrm{d}Y_t=\mathscr{G}(\theta)(t)\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma(t)\,\mathrm{d}B_t\), the coefficient is identified by the quadratic variation, the likelihood ratio for \(\theta\) is the Girsanov density, and the sufficient statistic for \(\theta\) is again the adjoint evolution driven by the data, now with the data measure replaced by \(\mathrm{d}Y_t/\sigma^2(t)\).
