Open Question 17.21, page 381 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: open.
Statement. Open question. Let \(\Omega=[0,1]^d\) be the torus, \(T>0\) and \(\mathcal{X}=[0,T]\times\Omega\), and let the data be \(Y_i=u_\theta(X_i)+\varepsilon_i\) at independent uniform space time points \(X_i\in\mathcal{X}\), with Gaussian noise \(\varepsilon_i\) and \(u_\theta=\mathscr{G}(\theta)\) the solution of an evolution equation with initial condition \(\theta\), the true initial condition being \(\theta_0\), as in the book’s transfer theorem for generative Bayesian computation (GBC) (catalog entry bvm_for_gbc): if the GBC posterior approximates the exact posterior with an error of smaller order than \(N^{-1/2}\) in Wasserstein distance and concentrates on the localization set of Nickl’s proof, it has the Gaussian limit of the exact posterior for the initial condition, together with the further conclusions about the trajectory, coverage and efficiency listed in that entry. This theorem and the Bernstein von Mises theorems of Nickl (2024) and of Konen and Nickl (2026) on which it rests assume deterministic dynamics without model error: every posterior draw is a solution of the equation and lies on the solution manifold \(\mathcal{M}=\{u_\theta\}\), and a trajectory generated with model error does not lie on \(\mathcal{M}\). In the state space formulation of Carlin, Polson and Stoffer (1992) the dynamics with model error are \(u_{k+1}=u_k+\Delta t\,F(u_k)+\sqrt{\Delta t}\,G\xi_k\), with time step \(\Delta t\), \(F\) the right hand side of the equation, innovations \(\xi_k\) and noise scale \(G\). The Gibbs smoother of Carlin, Polson and Stoffer is then the smoother for the initial condition problem: the forward edge \(p(u_{k+1}\mid u_k)\) is nonlinear in \(u_k\) through \(F\), the backward edge is Gaussian in \(u_k\), and a single move update samples \(u_k\) from their product. As \(G\to0\) the chain of transitions collapses to the deterministic solution map and the smoother degenerates to a sampler for \(\theta\) alone, which is the setting of Konen and Nickl (2026).
The Bayesian calibration framework of Kennedy and O’Hagan (2001), as made operational by Higdon and coauthors, runs the simulator at a design, fits a Gaussian process emulator of \(\theta\mapsto\mathscr{G}(\theta)\), adds a discrepancy process \(\delta\) and runs Markov chain Monte Carlo on \((\theta,\delta)\). The identifiability problem between \(\theta\) and \(\delta\) (Brynjarsdóttir and O’Hagan (2014); Tuo and Wu (2016)) is Condition 2E of Nickl (2024), the stability estimate \(\|\mathscr{G}(\theta)-\mathscr{G}(\theta_0)\|_{L^2(\mathcal{X})}\ge c\|\theta-\theta_0\|_{H^{-1}}\), in applied form: when the discrepancy can absorb a perturbation of \(\theta\), the information operator is not injective. The natural formulation is hierarchical, with \(\delta\) a Gaussian process of amplitude \(\sigma_N\to0\); for GBC it is trivial to include \(\delta\) in the simulation of the training pairs, and for the theory the admissible rate of \(\sigma_N\) is open.
Combine the transfer theorem with a discrepancy process of amplitude \(\sigma_N\) and identify the rate at which \(\sigma_N\) must tend to zero for the deterministic limit (the Gaussian limit of that theorem for dynamics without model error) to persist, connecting to the Gibbs smoother above and to the particle methods for state space models with static parameters (Storvik (2002); Carvalho, Johannes, Lopes and Polson (2010)). In the linear model without a latent state these particle systems collapse (the sufficient statistic is a deterministic function of the data, all weights are equal and there is nothing to resample), whereas with \(G\ne0\) the statistic depends on the sampled path, the weights are no longer equal, and the degeneracy of particles can occur.

title: Results by chapter On Hilbert’s 6th Problem
text:
Proposition 20.5, page 415 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. First stated in Carvalho, Johannes, Lopes and Polson (2010), Particle learning and smoothing, Statistical Science 25, 88 to 106.
Status: proved.
Statement. Consider a state space model with a static parameter \(\theta\), hidden states \(x_t\) and observations \(y_t\), with the Markov structure of such a model: \(y_{t+1}\) depends on the past only through the essential state \(z_t=(x_t,s_t,\theta)\), and \(p(x_{t+1}\mid z_t,y_{1:t+1})=p(x_{t+1}\mid z_t,y_{t+1})\). Suppose there are conditional sufficient statistics \(s_t\), updated deterministically by \(s_{t+1}=S(s_t,x_t,x_{t+1},y_{t+1})\), such that \(p(\theta\mid x_{0:t},y_{1:t})=p(\theta\mid s_t)\). Particle learning updates the essential state in four steps: (1) resample \(z_t\) with weights proportional to the predictive likelihood \(p(y_{t+1}\mid z_t)=\int p(y_{t+1}\mid x_{t+1},\theta)\,p(x_{t+1}\mid x_t,\theta)\,\mathrm{d}x_{t+1}\); (2) propagate \(x_{t+1}\sim p(x_{t+1}\mid z_t,y_{t+1})\); (3) update \(s_{t+1}=S(s_t,x_t,x_{t+1},y_{t+1})\); (4) draw \(\theta\sim p(\theta\mid s_{t+1})\). Let \(z_t\) have the law \(p(z_t\mid y_{1:t})\). Reweight this law by the predictive likelihood \(p(y_{t+1}\mid z_t)\), which is step one at the level of laws, and then apply steps two to four. Then the new essential state \((x_{t+1},s_{t+1},\theta)\) has the law \(p(x_{t+1},s_{t+1},\theta\mid y_{1:t+1})\).
Source: source/chapters/ext/ch14_pl.tex, label prop:pl_exact.




Theorem 20.9, page 423 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let the input spikes \(t_k\) form a Poisson process of rate \(\lambda>0\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). Attach to the \(k\)th spike a mark \((\tau_k,\kappa_k)\), the marks being independent with a common law \(M\) on \((0,\infty)^2\) and independent of the spike times, and given the marks let the amplitude \(A_k\) be exponential with rate \(\kappa_k\). Let \(V=\sum_{t_k\le t}A_k e^{-(t-t_k)/\tau_k}\) be the stationary potential at time \(t\). Then for every \(\theta>0\), with both sides possibly equal to \(+\infty\), \(-\log\mathbb{E}\,e^{-\theta V}=\lambda\int\tau\log\big(1+\theta/\kappa\big)\,M(\mathrm{d}\tau,\mathrm{d}\kappa)=\int\log\big(1+\theta/y\big)\,U(\mathrm{d}y)\), where \(U\) is the image of the measure \(\lambda\tau\,M(\mathrm{d}\tau,\mathrm{d}\kappa)\) under \((\tau,\kappa)\mapsto\kappa\). If \(\int\log(1+1/y)\,U(\mathrm{d}y)<\infty\), which is the condition that \(U\) be a Thorin measure, then \(V\) is a generalized Gamma convolution with Thorin measure \(U\) and zero drift, that is, \(\mathbb{E}\,e^{-\theta V}=\exp\big(-\int\log(1+\theta/y)\,U(\mathrm{d}y)\big)\) for \(\theta>0\). Otherwise \(V=\infty\) almost surely. In particular, if all marks equal \((\tau,\kappa)\) then \(V\) has the Gamma law with shape \(\lambda\tau\) and rate \(\kappa\), and if \(\tau_k\) and \(\kappa_k\) are independent and \(\kappa_k\) has law \(\nu\) then \(U=\lambda\,\mathbb{E}[\tau_k]\,\nu\).
Source: source/chapters/ch14_filters.tex, label thm:shot_noise_neuron.

title: Results by chapter On Hilbert’s 6th Problem
text:
Open Problem 1, page 445 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: open.
Statement. This is a program, and its first task is to fix the regime. Consider hard spheres in the Boltzmann Grad limit with Gibbs initial data conditioned on a macroscopic density, velocity and temperature profile, observed through the hydrodynamic fields at a later time with noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\). Find a relation between \(\sigma\), the Knudsen number and the number of particles under which the deviation of the particle fields from the solution of the limiting fluid equations is small compared with \(\sigma\), and prove under it a Bernstein von Mises theorem for smooth functionals of the initial macroscopic profile, with constants that do not depend on the number of particles.
Source: source/chapters/ch16_open.tex, label prob:inferential_sixth.




Open Problem 2, page 445 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: open.
Statement. Give quantitative versions of the method of arbitrary functions (for a real random variable \(X\) with a density \(g\) of total variation \(V<\infty\), \(t>0\) and \(a\in[0,1]\), \(|\mathbb{P}(\{tX\}\in[0,a))-a|\le a(1-a)V/(2t)\), where \(\{\cdot\}\) is the fractional part) for mixed phase space systems such as Hénon Heiles, where invariant tori and chaotic regions coexist, with rates in terms of the measure of the chaotic sea.
Source: source/chapters/ch16_open.tex, label prob:poincare.




Open Problem 3, page 445 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: open.
Statement. Quantitative estimates for chaos and entropic chaos in Kac’s model are known in several forms. Carlen, Carvalho, Le Roux, Loss and Villani (2010) relate propagation of chaos to entropy and show, in particular, that the entropic rate of convergence to equilibrium can be arbitrarily slow. Hauray and Mischler (2014) compare Kac’s chaos, entropic chaos and Fisher information chaos quantitatively, extend the estimates to measures on the Kac spheres, and treat mixtures in the sense of de Finetti, Hewitt and Savage. We do not know whether these estimates are optimal. Find the optimal rate, as a function of the marginal size \(k\) and of \(N\), in the finite de Finetti theorem for exchangeable laws on the sphere \(S^{N-1}(\sqrt N)\) in relative entropy, with examples showing that it cannot be improved, and use it to prove a propagation of chaos theorem for Kac’s model whose dependence on \(N\) is optimal under explicit hypotheses on the initial law.
Source: source/chapters/ch16_open.tex, label prob:axioms.




Open Problem 4, page 445 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: open.
Statement. Open problem, posed as a program in the book. Kent’s theorem writes the hitting time of a level \(b\) by a regular one dimensional diffusion, started at a reflecting or entrance boundary \(a\), as \(\sum_{n\geq1}E_n/\lambda_n\), where \(E_1,E_2,\dots\) are independent standard exponential variables and \(0<\lambda_1<\lambda_2<\cdots\) are the eigenvalues of minus the generator on \((a,b)\) with Dirichlet condition at \(b\) and the reflecting or entrance condition at \(a\). For each \(n\), the remainder \(\sum_{k>n}E_k/\lambda_k\) after the first \(n\) terms is a generalized Gamma convolution (a law on \([0,\infty)\) with Laplace transform \(s\mapsto e^{-\phi(s)}\), \(\phi(s)=cs+\int_{(0,\infty)}\log(1+s/y)\,U(\mathrm{d}y)\), where \(c\geq0\) and \(U\) is the Thorin measure) with an explicit Thorin measure. The problem is to identify a class of regular diffusions for which this remainder can be sampled exactly with finite expected cost, to prove that the resulting sampler is exact, and to use it to build a library of exact samplers for Brownian functionals.
Source: source/chapters/ch16_open.tex, label prob:yor.




Open Problem 5, page 445 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: open.
Statement. Let \(\xi(s)=\frac12 s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)\), \(\Xi(x)=\xi(\frac12+ix)\) and \(\Phi(u)=\sum_{n\ge1}\big(2\pi^2n^4e^{9u}-3\pi n^2e^{5u}\big)\exp(-\pi n^2e^{4u})\), so that \(\Xi(x)=8\int_0^\infty\Phi(u)\cos(2xu)\,\mathrm{d}u\). The Pólya law is the law of a random variable \(X\) with the symmetric density \(\Phi(|u|)/\int_{\mathbb{R}}\Phi(|v|)\,\mathrm{d}v\); its moment generating function is \(\mathbb{E}e^{sX}=\Xi(-is/2)/\Xi(0)\). By Khintchine’s theorem the Pólya law is the law of \(UZ\) with \(U\) uniform on \([-1,1]\) and \(Z\ge0\) independent of \(U\). The law of \(Z\) is not a generalized Gamma convolution, because \(Z\) has finite exponential moments of every order and a nonconstant generalized Gamma convolution does not. The reciprocal of the moment generating function of \(UZ\) at \(2\sqrt\lambda\) is a different matter. It is \(\Xi(0)/\Xi(i\sqrt\lambda)=\prod_n(1+\lambda/\gamma_n^2)^{-1}\), where \(\pm\gamma_n\) are the zeros of \(\Xi\), and it is the Laplace transform of a generalized Gamma convolution (a law on \([0,\infty)\) with Laplace transform \(\exp\{-as-\int_{(0,\infty)}\log(1+s/t)\,U(\mathrm{d}t)\}\), \(a\ge0\), \(U\) the Thorin measure) if and only if the Riemann hypothesis holds. In that case the Thorin measure is the sum of point masses at the \(\gamma_n^2\). Conversely, the logarithmic derivative of the Laplace transform of a generalized Gamma convolution is analytic outside the negative half line, which forces all the \(\gamma_n^2\) to be positive. Prove that this function is the Laplace transform of a generalized Gamma convolution by using the mixture representation \(X=UZ\) and not the location of the zeros.
Source: source/chapters/ch16_open.tex, label prob:mixtures.




Open Problem 6, page 446 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: open.
Statement. For a probability density \(u_0\) of finite variance on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) let \(u_\tau\) solve the heat equation \(\partial_\tau u=\Delta u\), and let \(W(\tau)=\tau J(u_\tau)+h(u_\tau)-\frac n2\log(4\pi\tau)-n\), where \(J(u)=\int|\nabla u|^2/u\) is the Fisher information and \(h(u)=-\int u\log u\) the differential entropy; \(W\) is nonincreasing. Ni (2004) proved that the analog of \(W\) for the linear heat equation on a Riemannian manifold is nonincreasing when the Ricci curvature is nonnegative. Extend the scale mixture proof of the monotonicity of \(W\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (for initial densities \(u_0=\int\varphi_v\,G(\mathrm{d}v)\), mixtures of the centered Gaussian densities \(\varphi_v\) with covariance \(vI\) under a mixing law \(G\), for which \(u_\tau=\int\varphi_{v+2\tau}\,G(\mathrm{d}v)\)) to Riemannian manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature, interpreting the Ricci term as a correction to the subordinated Brownian motion.
Source: source/chapters/ch16_open.tex, label prob:perelman.




Open Problem 7, page 446 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: open.
Statement. Formulate a prior on Nelson’s diffusions (diffusions with diffusion constant \(\hbar/2m\) whose drift is determined by the density \(\rho\) and the phase \(S\) of a wave function \(\psi=\sqrt\rho\,e^{iS/\hbar}\)) that does not itself impose the quantization condition, and identify data that determine the circulation of the drift around the nodes of the density, so that the posterior concentrates on drifts satisfying the quantization condition. Position statistics alone fix the density and, through the continuity equation, only the divergence of the current, so the data must carry more. A solution would give a Bayesian answer to Wallstrom’s objection. Wallstrom (1994) observed that the condition that \(\psi\) be single valued, which forces the quantization of angular momentum, does not follow from Nelson’s equations, which only involve \(\rho\) and \(\nabla S\); it must be added by hand.
Source: source/chapters/ch16_open.tex, label prob:quantum.




Open Problem 8, page 446 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: open.
Statement. Open problem. Consider the Kac walk with \(N\) particles and total collision rate \(N\): the velocities \(v=(v_1,\dots,v_N)\) lie on the sphere \(S^{N-1}(\sqrt N)=\{\sum_{i\leq N}v_i^2=N\}\), and at rate \(N\) a pair \((i,j)\) is chosen uniformly and an angle \(\theta\) uniformly on \([0,2\pi)\), and the pair is rotated by \(\theta\). Let \(\sigma_N\) be the uniform probability law on the sphere. For a probability density \(F\) with respect to \(\sigma_N\) let \(H_N(F)=\int F\log F\,\mathrm{d}\sigma_N\) be its relative entropy with respect to \(\sigma_N\), and let \(D_N(F)=-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}H_N(F_t)\big|_{t=0}\) be the rate at which \(H_N\) decreases at time zero along the master equation of the walk, where \(F_t\) is the solution started at \(F_0=F\). For comparison, Villani’s argument gives \(D_N(F)\geq2H_N(F)/(N-1)\) for every \(F\), and Gao, Wang and Xia state in a 2026 preprint that \(2/(N-1)\) is the best constant over all \(F\). For a probability density \(f\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) let \(Z_N(f)=\int\prod_{i\leq N}f(v_i)\,\sigma_N(\mathrm{d}v)\) and \(F^f_N(v)=Z_N(f)^{-1}\prod_{i\leq N}f(v_i)\). Fix \(M>3\) and let \(\mathcal{G}_M\) be the set of bounded probability densities \(f\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) that are normal scale mixtures, \(f(v)=\int(2\pi s)^{-1/2}e^{-v^2/(2s)}\,G(\mathrm{d}s)\) with a mixing law \(G\) on \([0,\infty)\) that is a generalized Gamma convolution (a law on \([0,\infty)\) with Laplace transform \(\exp(-cs-\int_{(0,\infty)}\log(1+s/y)\,U(\mathrm{d}y))\) for some \(c\geq0\) and some measure \(U\) on \((0,\infty)\) with \(\int\log(1+1/y)\,U(\mathrm{d}y)<\infty\), the Thorin measure), and that satisfy \(\int v^2f(v)\,\mathrm{d}v=1\) and \(\int v^4f(v)\,\mathrm{d}v\leq M\). The question is whether there is \(\lambda>0\), depending only on \(M\), such that \(D_N(F^f_N)\geq\lambda H_N(F^f_N)\) for every \(N\geq2\) and every \(f\in\mathcal{G}_M\).
Source: source/chapters/ch16_open.tex, label prob:kinetic.




Open Problem 10, page 447 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: open.
Statement. Open problem. Konen and Nickl prove a functional Bernstein von Mises theorem for the posterior of the trajectory of the two dimensional Navier Stokes equations on the torus, with root \(N\) consistent prediction of future states in the supremum norm, for a Gaussian prior on the initial condition and \(N\) noisy observations at uniformly random points of space and time. The authors know of no corresponding result for sensors at fixed locations or for other priors. The problem is to determine the posterior contraction rate for the initial vorticity from noisy point observations at a fixed array of sensors and times, in terms of the number of sensors, the number of times and the noise level, and to identify the functionals of the initial vorticity that admit a Bernstein von Mises theorem. A companion question is whether the posterior of the initial vorticity can be computed in time polynomial in the data size and the dimension.
Source: source/chapters/ch16_open.tex, label prob:inference.




Open Problem 11, page 447 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: open.
Statement. Fix a finite horizon and a computable blowup criterion, for example that a norm of the solution of a Galerkin truncation of the equations exceeds a threshold before the horizon. Construct a prior on initial data and forcing for three dimensional Navier Stokes and a sequence of numerical solvers such that the posterior probability of this event is consistent, that is, converges to its true value as the resolution and the amount of data increase, and quantify how the event approximates finite time blowup of the exact solution. Consistency for the blowup of the exact solution itself, under either hypothesis, would require deciding the regularity of the data near the truth, which is the regularity problem.
Source: source/chapters/ch16_open.tex, label prob:blowup.




Open Problem 12, page 447 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: open.
Statement. This is a program. At finite Reynolds number the velocity field is smooth, so a Hölder exponent has to be defined through an inertial range statement, such as the scaling \(S_p(\ell)\propto\ell^{\zeta_p}\) of the structure functions. Develop a joint posterior for the exponents \(\zeta_p\) and the inertial range from measured velocity increments, and use it to ask whether laboratory and numerical data concentrate at, above or below the exponents \(\zeta_p=p/3\) of Kolmogorov and Onsager.
Source: source/chapters/ch16_open.tex, label prob:onsager.




Open Problem 13, page 448 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: open.
Statement. Consider the planted clique problem with a known clique size \(k\) in the graph \(G(n,\frac12)\). The book records that approximate message passing succeeds for \(k\ge(1+\varepsilon)\sqrt{n/e}\), and that from a suitable starting state the Metropolis process cannot find a planted clique of size \(k=n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\) in polynomial time. Take as samplers of the posterior over clique locations either Glauber dynamics on vertex sets of size \(k\), or Langevin dynamics for a continuous relaxation of the clique indicator, in both cases initialized from the prior. Determine whether such samplers have a computational phase transition at \(k=\sqrt{n/e}\), in the sense that they succeed in polynomial time above \((1+\varepsilon)\sqrt{n/e}\) and fail below \((1-\varepsilon)\sqrt{n/e}\).
Source: source/chapters/ch16_open.tex, label prob:phase_transitions.




Open Problem 14, page 448 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: open.
Statement. Prove convergence rates for generative Bayesian computation via learned Schrödinger bridges in terms of the entropic regularization, the number of simulations and the smoothness of the posterior. Rates in the sample size are known for the entropic optimal transport cost estimated from samples, by Genevay, Chizat, Bach, Cuturi and Peyré (2019) and by Mena and Niles Weed (2019). The problem concerns the learned bridge as an estimator of the posterior.
Source: source/chapters/ch16_open.tex, label prob:transport.




Open Problem 15, page 448 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: open.
Statement. The Landauer bound bounds the heat dissipated by a physical process in terms of the entropy removed, and the Sagawa Ueda inequality bounds the work in terms of the mutual information acquired. For a Bayesian update from a prior \(\mu_0\) to the posterior \(\mu_y\), prove a lower bound on the heat dissipated by any physical implementation in terms of \(\mathrm{KL}(\mu_y\|\mu_0)\) and the information erased, and compare it with the dissipation of Langevin samplers.
Source: source/chapters/ch16_open.tex, label prob:thermodynamics_of_inference.




Open Problem 16, page 448 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: open.
Statement. This is a program whose goal is the Riemann hypothesis. Let \(\xi(s)=\frac12 s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)\), \(\Xi(x)=\xi(\frac12+ix)\) and \(\Phi(u)=\sum_{n\ge1}\big(2\pi^2n^4e^{9u}-3\pi n^2e^{5u}\big)\exp(-\pi n^2e^{4u})\), so that \(\Xi(x)=8\int_0^\infty\Phi(u)\cos(2xu)\,\mathrm{d}u\). The Pólya law is the law with the symmetric density \(\Phi(|u|)/\int_{\mathbb{R}}\Phi(|v|)\,\mathrm{d}v\); its moment generating function is \(\Xi(-is/2)/\Xi(0)\). The de Bruijn Newman constant \(\Lambda\) is the real number such that \(H_t(z)=\int_0^\infty e^{tu^2}\Phi(u)\cos(zu)\,\mathrm{d}u\) has only real zeros if and only if \(t\ge\Lambda\), and the Riemann hypothesis is equivalent to \(\Lambda\le0\). A symmetric random variable \(X\) with \(\mathbb{E}e^{bX^2}<\infty\) for every \(b>0\) has the Lee Yang property if \(z\mapsto\mathbb{E}e^{zX}\) has only purely imaginary zeros; the uniform law on \([-1,1]\) and the Ising spin \(\pm1\) have it. Newman’s theorem (1974): if \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are independent with the Lee Yang property, \(J_{ij}\ge0\) are such that \(\exp(\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}x_ix_j)\) is integrable against the product law, and \(\mathbb{P}_J\) has density proportional to this exponential with respect to the product law, then \(\sum_ia_iX_i\) under \(\mathbb{P}_J\) has the Lee Yang property for every choice of positive weights \(a_i\). The Riemann hypothesis holds if and only if the Pólya law has the Lee Yang property. Decide whether the Pólya law is the weak limit of a sequence of laws of random variables \(X_n\) obtained by such constructions from Ising spins and uniform laws, with \(\sup_n\mathbb{E}e^{c|X_n|}<\infty\) for every \(c>0\), which is the control that carries the Lee Yang property to the limit by Hurwitz’s theorem. A construction would prove the Riemann hypothesis, and a proof that none exists would show that this route to the hypothesis is closed.
Source: source/chapters/ch16_open.tex, label prob:bridge.

title: Clinical Trials in Practice From Foundations to AI Agents
text:
Description
On an open highway you can pass every other car and go fast. A clinical trial is like downtown driving. The pace is set by the traffic around you: regulators, sites, patients, and the protocol itself.
This book explains how that traffic moves and how to work with it. It follows a trial from the first idea to the regulatory submission and gives Phase III the most room, because that is where approval is won or lost. Statistics, operations and technology are taught side by side, because a design choice in the protocol becomes a task at the site, a field in the database and a document an inspector will ask to see.
Some of the questions it answers: When does a study need an IND, and what does an investigator take on by becoming the sponsor of one? How do you size a trial, plan interim analyses, and decide whether an adaptive or Bayesian design is worth the extra planning? When can real world evidence or an external control arm support a regulatory decision? Why does a site that predicts 30 patients sometimes enroll 3, and how should a sponsor read feasibility data? What does an academic multi-site trial need from its coordinating center, and what does a site new to research, rural or urban, usually lack? What does risk-based monitoring change about a monitor’s work? What has to be in the trial master file when the inspector arrives?
The chapters run in the order a development program does. They begin with how clinical research took its present shape, from the Elixir Sulfanilamide deaths of 1937 to ICH E6(R3) Good Clinical Practice, and with the ethics of research with human subjects. They follow a compound through development economics and Phases I to IV. The Phase III part covers statistical methods, adaptive and Bayesian trial design with platform trials such as I-SPY 2 and REMAP-CAP, study design and protocol complexity, randomization and blinding, endpoints and estimands, site selection, patient recruitment and retention, logistics and project management, data management and EDC, clinical monitoring, safety reporting, essential documents and the trial master file, and the IT systems underneath. The last chapters cover closeout, the clinical study report, and regulatory submission, including expedited pathways and FDA inspections.
The chapter on AI agents treats an agent as one more computerized system that must survive an inspection. It sets out what FDA and EMA guidance allows today, such as TMF filing, query generation and eligibility prescreening as decision support, and what it does not allow, such as replacing the investigator’s judgment. It describes how structured, machine-readable protocols (ICH M11, CDISC USDM) connect the protocol to data collection, and it says plainly where no measured evidence exists yet. Every use it describes needs validation, an audit trail and a named person accountable for each decision.
It is written for medical directors, study managers and monitors; for investigators and site coordinators, including those running their own investigator-initiated trials; for statisticians who want to see how a design plays out in practice; and for students and informatics and AI engineers who need to know how regulated research works before they build tools for it.

Proposition 21.4, page 433 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On Hilbert’s 6th Problem: Probability, Mechanics and Bayesian Computation, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \(\Theta\) be a target and let \(M_0\) be a model with \(I(\Theta;M_0)=i_0\), where \(I\) denotes mutual information. Suppose \(M_{k+1}\) is computed from \(M_k\) and from fresh randomness independent of \(\Theta\). Then \(I(\Theta;M_k)\le i_0\) for all \(k\). If at each round the update also uses the output of a verifier \(V_k\) that depends on \(\Theta\) through a channel of capacity \(C\) bits per round, so that \(I(\Theta;V_k\mid M_k)\le C\), then \(I(\Theta;M_k)\le i_0+kC\).

title: On the Collatz Conjecture Martingales, Momentum and Continued Fractions
text:
Description
The Collatz conjecture says that, from any positive integer, repeatedly halving an even number and sending an odd number n to 3n+1 always reaches 1. This book explains why the problem has resisted proof. It reads the map as a random walk, as an optimization algorithm and as a problem in Diophantine approximation, and it makes each obstruction precise.
The conjecture splits into a divergence half, a law of large numbers along a single deterministic orbit, and a cycle half, a question about rational approximation of log2 3 that Diophantine information alone cannot finish. The book proves that no Lyapunov function increasing in the number certifies descent over any fixed number of steps, and that no finite residue sieve certifies descent for every integer. It proves that however far the computer verification is pushed, infinitely many cycle lengths survive the cycle inequality, so the inequality and the verification alone cannot exclude all cycles, a point Halbeisen and Hungerbühler made earlier in another form.
The arithmetic of the map also yields an algorithm. Switching MM, a first order method that applies the momentum log2 3 minus 1 on alternate steps, has an explicit linear rate at step 1/L on smooth strongly convex functions, and on quadratics with additive gradient noise, at steps up to 1/L, its noise variance stays below 5/3 times that of gradient descent for every momentum coefficient below one. The gain weight theorem shows that on quadratics with small steps no stable linear periodic first order method has a lower slow mode noise floor than gradient descent at matched speed.
Every result is proved in full or marked as conditional, the open problems are collected in the closing chapter, and the Python scripts behind every computed number, figure and table are in the repository.

title: On the Collatz Conjecture Martingales, Momentum and Continued Fractions
On the Collatz Conjecture Martingales, Momentum and Continued Fractions
text:
Main results

No fixed horizon monotone certificate for Collatz descent (Corollary 4.15, page 78): For every fixed number J of strides, no strictly increasing function of x certifies descent over J Syracuse strides, because the odd integers congruent to minus 1 modulo 2 to the J+1 ascend for J strides in a row.
Noise bound for Switching MM uniform in the normalized step (Proposition 8.7, page 130): On a quadratic with additive gradient noise, on every eigendirection with normalized step up to one, the stationary variance of Switching MM lies between that of gradient descent and 5/3 times it, uniformly over momentum coefficients below one, whereas every step momentum amplifies slow mode noise by a factor that grows without bound as the coefficient tends to one.
Gain weight theorem for the noise floor of periodic first order methods (Theorem 8.12, page 135): For any linear periodic first order method on a quadratic that is stable at zero normalized step and has positive total gain, the slow mode noise floor at matched speed relative to gradient descent is a Cauchy and Schwarz ratio of the step gains, at least one, and equal to one only when all gains are equal.
Exact linear rate of Switching MM on smooth strongly convex functions (Theorem 9.9, page 164): For strongly convex and L smooth functions, two steps of Switching MM at step one over L contract the distance to the minimizer by the product of the classical one step factors of a long and a short gradient step, which explicit functions show is the exact worst case over the class, and the function gap by its square, using the one step function value bound of Taylor, Hendrickx and Glineur (2018).
Diophantine insufficiency, infinitely many cycle lengths survive any verification range (Proposition 11.20, page 205): However far the verification of the Collatz conjecture is pushed, infinitely many cycle lengths survive the cycle inequality, so information about the approximation of log2 3 alone cannot exclude all nontrivial cycles, a point Halbeisen and Hungerbühler (1997) made earlier in another form.
Residue certificates cannot prove descent for all integers (the exceptional 2 adic set) (Proposition 15.1, page 267): No residue certificate of finite level can certify descent for every integer, because every residue class it leaves uncovered contains infinitely many positive integers, while the 2 adic integers with infinite coefficient stopping time form a closed null set that contains a point of each known negative cycle.

Status: proved; conditional (proved assuming the named statements, which the book does not prove); open (stated as an open question); counterexample (a proved counterexample); withdrawn (found wrong after release; the entry says what was wrong and which version corrects it).





Proposition 3.7, page 48 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On the Collatz Conjecture: Martingales, Momentum and Continued Fractions, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \((B_n)_{n\ge0}\) be the Markov chain on \(\{0,1\}\) with \(\mathbb{P}(B_{n+1}=0\mid B_n=1)=1\) and \(\mathbb{P}(B_{n+1}=0\mid B_n=0)=\mathbb{P}(B_{n+1}=1\mid B_n=0)=\tfrac12\), let \(x_0>0\), and put \(x_{n+1}=3x_n\) if \(B_n=1\) and \(x_{n+1}=x_n/2\) if \(B_n=0\), with \(\mathcal{F}_n=\sigma(B_0,\ldots,B_n)\) (the renewal model for the standard Collatz map, which sends an even \(m\) to \(m/2\) and an odd \(m\) to \(3m+1\), where \(B_n\) models the parity of the \(n\)th iterate). Write \(\delta^{*}=\log(\sqrt3/2)\). Then (i) the stationary law of the chain satisfies \(\mathbb{P}(B_n=1)=\tfrac13\), and the fraction of odd steps (indices \(i\) with \(B_i=1\)) among the first \(n\) steps converges to \(\tfrac13\) almost surely from any initial state; (ii) \((x_n)\) is not a martingale, since \(\mathbb{E}[x_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]=3x_n\) on \(\{B_n=1\}\), but \(M_n=3^{B_n}x_n\) is a martingale; (iii) \((\log x_n)\) is not a supermartingale, since its increment is \(+\log3\) on \(\{B_n=1\}\), but \(\log M_n\) is a supermartingale with conditional drift \(0\) on \(\{B_n=1\}\) and \(\delta^{*}\) on \(\{B_n=0\}\); (iv) almost surely \(\frac1n\log x_n\to\tfrac13\log3 - \tfrac23\log2=\tfrac13\log\tfrac34=\tfrac23\delta^{*}\approx -0.0959\); (v) if \(\tau_1<\tau_2<\cdots\) are the successive times at which \(B_n=1\), then \(X_j=x_{\tau_j}\) satisfies \(X_{j+1}=3X_j2^{-K_{j+1}}\), where \(K_{j+1}=\tau_{j+1} - \tau_j - 1\) are independent with the Geometric\((\tfrac12)\) law \(\mathbb{P}(K=k)=2^{-k}\) for \(k\ge1\), and \((X_j)\) is a martingale because \(\mathbb{E}[3\cdot2^{-K}]=3\sum_{k\ge1}4^{-k}=1\).
Source: book/chapters/ch03_stochastic.tex, label prop:ch3:standard.




Proposition 3.12, page 56 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On the Collatz Conjecture: Martingales, Momentum and Continued Fractions, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \((B_n)_{n\ge0}\) be the Markov chain on \(\{0,1\}\) with \(\mathbb{P}(B_{n+1}=0\mid B_n=1)=1\) and \(\mathbb{P}(B_{n+1}=0\mid B_n=0)=\mathbb{P}(B_{n+1}=1\mid B_n=0)=\tfrac12\) (the renewal model for the standard Collatz map, where \(B_n\) models the parity of the \(n\)th iterate), started from its stationary law. Then \((B_n)\) is stationary with \(\mathbb{P}(B_n=1)=\frac{1}{1+\mathbb{E}[K]}=\frac13\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(B_n)=\frac29\), where \(K\), the number of zeros between successive ones of the chain, has the Geometric\((\tfrac12)\) law \(\mathbb{P}(K=k)=2^{-k}\) for \(k\ge1\) (so \(\mathbb{E}[K]=2\)), and its autocorrelation function is \(\rho(h)=\operatorname{Corr}(B_n,B_{n+h})=\bigl(-\tfrac12\bigr)^{h}\) for \(h\ge0\).
Source: book/chapters/ch03_stochastic.tex, label thm:autocorr.




Corollary 3.14, page 58 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On the Collatz Conjecture: Martingales, Momentum and Continued Fractions, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \((B_n)_{n\ge0}\) be the Markov chain on \(\{0,1\}\) with \(\mathbb{P}(B_{n+1}=0\mid B_n=1)=1\) and \(\mathbb{P}(B_{n+1}=0\mid B_n=0)=\mathbb{P}(B_{n+1}=1\mid B_n=0)=\tfrac12\), started from any initial state, let \(x_0>0\), and put \(x_{n+1}=3x_n\) if \(B_n=1\) and \(x_{n+1}=x_n/2\) if \(B_n=0\) (the renewal model for the standard Collatz map). Let \(\rho(h)=(-\tfrac12)^h\) be the autocorrelation function of \((B_n)\). The autocorrelation factor is \(\mathcal{A}:=1+2\sum_{h\ge1}\rho(h)=1+2\cdot\frac{-1/2}{1+1/2}=\frac13\), and the variance of the log path satisfies \(\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\log x_n)}{n}\longrightarrow\mathcal{A}\cdot\frac29(\log6)^2=\frac{2}{27}(\log6)^2\approx0.2378\) as \(n\to\infty\).

Proposition 3.17, page 61 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On the Collatz Conjecture: Martingales, Momentum and Continued Fractions, edition 1. New in this book.

Statement. Then \(\tau<\infty\) almost surely, the stopped process \((x_{n\wedge\tau})_{n\ge0}\) is a nonnegative martingale converging almost surely to \(x_\tau\le1\), and it is not uniformly integrable. More precisely, for every \(n\), \(\mathbb{E}\bigl[x_n\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau>n\}}\bigr]\ge x_0 - 1\), while \(\mathbb{P}(\tau>n)\to0\) as \(n\to\infty\).

Proposition 4.5, page 70 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On the Collatz Conjecture: Martingales, Momentum and Continued Fractions, edition 1. New in this book.

Theorem 4.7, page 71 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On the Collatz Conjecture: Martingales, Momentum and Continued Fractions, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \(S\) be the Syracuse map on the odd positive integers, \(S(x)=(3x+1)/2^{k}\) with \(k=v_2(3x+1)\), where \(v_2(m)\) is the exponent of the largest power of \(2\) dividing \(m\). Let \(x\ge3\) be odd and \(k=v_2(3x+1)\). (i) \(\log S(x)-\log x=\log(3+1/x)-k\log2\). (ii) If \(k\ge2\), then \(S(x)<x\), \(\log S(x)-\log x\le\log\bigl(\tfrac34+\tfrac1{4x}\bigr)<0\), and \(\log S(x)-\log x\le\log(7/9)\), with equality exactly at \(x=9\). (iii) If \(k=1\), which happens exactly when \(x\equiv3\pmod4\), then \(S(x)=(3x+1)/2>x\) and \(\log\tfrac32<\log S(x)-\log x=\log\bigl(\tfrac32+\tfrac1{2x}\bigr)\le\log\tfrac53\), with equality on the right exactly at \(x=3\).

Theorem 4.8, page 73 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On the Collatz Conjecture: Martingales, Momentum and Continued Fractions, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \(S\) be the Syracuse map on the odd positive integers, \(S(x)=(3x+1)/2^{v_2(3x+1)}\), where \(v_2(m)\) is the exponent of the largest power of \(2\) dividing \(m\). Let \(W\) be a strictly increasing function from the odd positive integers to \((0,\infty)\), and let \(\rho\le1\). Then \(W(S(x))>\rho\,W(x)\) for every \(x\equiv3\pmod4\). In particular no strictly increasing \(W\) is a strict Lyapunov function for \((S,\{1\})\) (one with \(W(S(x))<W(x)\) for every odd \(x\ne1\)) or a strong Lyapunov function for \((S,\{1\})\) (one with \(W>0\) and \(W(S(x))\le\rho W(x)\) for every odd \(x\ne1\), for some constant \(\rho<1\)), and the set of odd integers on which \(W(S(x))\le\rho W(x)\) fails contains the residue class \(3\bmod4\), which has natural density \(\tfrac12\) among the odd integers; for \(\rho=1\) the set on which it fails is exactly this class.

Proposition 4.12, page 74 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On the Collatz Conjecture: Martingales, Momentum and Continued Fractions, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \(S\) be the Syracuse map on the odd positive integers, \(S(x)=(3x+1)/2^{v_2(3x+1)}\), where \(v_2(m)\) is the exponent of the largest power of \(2\) dividing \(m\). For odd \(x\) write \(k_1=v_2(3x+1)\), \(k_2=v_2(3S(x)+1)\) and \(S^{(2)}(x)=S(S(x))\). Let \(x\ge3\) be odd. (i) \(S^{(2)}(x)<x\) if and only if \(k_1+k_2\ge4\). (ii) The odd integers with a two stride descent, that is with \(S^{(2)}(x)<x\), have natural density exactly \(\tfrac12\) among the odd integers. (iii) \(\max_{x\ge3\text{ odd}}\bigl(\log S^{(2)}(x)-\log x\bigr)=\log\tfrac{17}{7}\approx0.8873\), attained only at \(x=7\), where \(S(7)=11\) and \(S^{(2)}(7)=17\).

Corollary 4.15, page 78 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On the Collatz Conjecture: Martingales, Momentum and Continued Fractions, edition 1. New in this book.

Statement. Fix \(J\ge1\), \(\rho\le1\) and a strictly increasing function \(W\) from the odd positive integers to \((0,\infty)\). Then \(W(S^{(J)}(x))>\rho\,W(x)\) for every odd \(x\equiv-1\pmod{2^{J+1}}\), that is, for every \(x=2^{J+1}q-1\) with \(q\ge1\). This set is infinite and has natural density \(2^{-J}\) among the odd integers. Moreover, along it, [()^{J}(q).]

Proposition 4.19, page 79 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On the Collatz Conjecture: Martingales, Momentum and Continued Fractions, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \(T_0\) be the standard Collatz map, \(T_0(x)=x/2\) for even \(x\) and \(T_0(x)=3x+1\) for odd \(x\), and let \(g(y\mid x)=\log x+(y-x)/x\) be the tangent line majorizer of \(\log\) at \(x\), so that the surrogate increment \(g(T_0(x)\mid x)-g(x\mid x)\) equals \(-\tfrac12\) for even \(x\) and \(2+1/x\) for odd \(x\). Under the stochastic model for the standard map, in which the parities of successive steps form a stationary renewal chain \((B_n)\) on \(\{0,1\}\) (with \(B_n=1\) for an odd step; an odd step is always followed by an even step, and an even step is followed by an odd or an even step with probability \(\tfrac12\) each), so that a step is odd with stationary probability \(\tfrac13\), the mean surrogate increment per step of \(T_0\) is \(\tfrac13\cdot2+\tfrac23\cdot\bigl(-\tfrac12\bigr)=+\tfrac13>0\), up to the \(O(1/x)\) term, whereas the mean true increment per step is \(\tfrac13\log3-\tfrac23\log2=\tfrac13\log(3/4)\approx-0.0959<0\). Per Syracuse stride, that is one odd step followed by \(k\) even steps, in the stride model with \(k\) distributed as Geometric\((\tfrac12)\) on \(\{1,2,\dots\}\), the per step surrogate increments summed over the stride, with the majorizer recentred at every step, have mean \(+1\) up to the \(O(1/x)\) term, and the mean true increment is \(\log(3/4)\approx-0.2877\).
Source: book/chapters/ch04_lyapunov.tex, label prop:mmfails.




Proposition 4.20, page 81 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On the Collatz Conjecture: Martingales, Momentum and Continued Fractions, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Work in the stride model of the Collatz map, in which the log increment of one stride is \(\Delta=\log3-K\log2\) with \(K\) distributed as Geometric\((\tfrac12)\) on \(\{1,2,\dots\}\), and write \(M(p)=\mathbb{E}[e^{p\Delta}]=3^{p}/(2^{1+p}-1)\). For \(0<p\le1\) let \(g_p(y\mid x)=\log x+\frac{(y/x)^{p}-1}{p}\); each \(g_p\) dominates \(\log y\) and is tangent to it at \(y=x\), and \(p=1\) is the tangent line (linear) majorizer of \(\log\). Then the mean stride increment of the surrogate \(g_p\), ignoring the \(1/x\) correction, is \((M(p)-1)/p\), and: (i) \(M(0)=M(1)=1\), and \(M(p)<1\) for \(0<p<1\); (ii) \(p\mapsto(M(p)-1)/p\) is increasing on \((0,1]\), tends to \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta]=\log(3/4)\) as \(p\downarrow0\), and equals \(0\) at \(p=1\). In particular every power majorizer with \(0<p<1\) has strictly negative mean surrogate increment, and the linear majorizer \(p=1\) sits exactly on the boundary.
Source: book/chapters/ch04_lyapunov.tex, label prop:ch4:power.







Theorem 6.3, page 101 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On the Collatz Conjecture: Martingales, Momentum and Continued Fractions, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \(T\) be the accelerated Collatz map, \(T(x)=x/2\) for even \(x\) and \(T(x)=(3x+1)/2\) for odd \(x\). Fix \(d\ge1\) and let \(G_d\) be the directed graph on the residues modulo \(2^d\) in which the residue \(a\) has an edge to each residue \(a'\) with \(a'\equiv T(a)\pmod{2^{d-1}}\) (the two lifts of \(T(a)\)), with weight \(w(a)=\log(3/2)\) if \(a\) is odd and \(w(a)=-\log2\) if \(a\) is even. (i) There are a function \(\varphi\) on \(\mathbb{Z}/2^d\mathbb{Z}\) and a bound \(X\) such that \(V(T(x))<V(x)\) for all integers \(x\ge X\), where \(V(x)=\log x+\varphi(x\bmod2^d)\), if and only if every cycle of \(G_d\) has negative total weight. (ii) For every \(d\ge1\) the graph \(G_d\) contains cycles of positive weight: the loop at \(-1\), of weight \(\log(3/2)\), and the images of the cycles of \(T\) on the negative integers, whose weights are \(r\log3-s\log2>0\) for a cycle with \(r\) odd steps among \(s\) steps. The maximum cycle mean of \(G_d\) is exactly \(\log(3/2)\) for every \(d\). (iii) Consequently no potential \(\log x+\varphi(x\bmod2^d)\) with bounded \(\varphi\) decreases at every step for all large \(x\), for any \(d\), and the same holds for potentials required to decrease over any fixed number \(J\) of steps.
Source: book/chapters/ch05c_mmcollatz.tex, label thm:ch5c:residue.




Proposition 6.4, page 102 of Polson and Sokolov (2026), On the Collatz Conjecture: Martingales, Momentum and Continued Fractions, edition 1. New in this book.
Status: proved.
Statement. Let \(S\) be the Syracuse map on the odd positive integers, \(S(x)=(3x+1)/2^{v_2(3x+1)}\), where \(v_2(m)\) is the exponent of the largest power of \(2\) dividing \(m\), and let \(V(x)=\log x+\varphi(x)\) for a real function \(\varphi\) on the odd positive integers. Suppose \(V(S(x))<V(x)\) for every odd \(x\ge3\). Then for every \(j\ge2\) and every odd \(q\ge1\), [(2jq-1)-(2{j-1}q-1);>;(j-1) .] In particular \(\varphi\) is unbounded above or below, and \(\sup\varphi-\inf\varphi\ge(j-1)\log(3/2)\) for every \(j\).
